Published: 15:37 EDT, 26 September 2026 | Updated: 15:40 EDT, 26 September 2026
A heavyhearted Rande Gerber was seen paying another visit to the Hollywood Hills home of his late son Presley.
The businessman, 64, arrived at the residence on Friday in a black Range Rover and then walked up to the front door with his head down and covered by a baseball cap, according to photographs obtained by the Daily Mail.
He was dressed in a blue T-shirt, white shorts and blue sneakers.
His wife, Cindy Crawford , 60, did not appear to be with him, but he had a male companion with him to help with whatever needed to be done as details of Presley's crippling trauma as a teenager come to light.
Gerber is said to have spent about three hours at the lushly landscaped property.
The Daily Mail has reached out to Crawford and Gerber's representatives for comment.
A heavyhearted Rande Gerber was seen on Friday paying another visit to the Hollywood Hills home of his late son Presley - days after the 27-year-old's shock death from a suspected overdose
Gerber is said to have spent about three hours at the lushly landscaped property
It's the second time this week that Gerber has been to the house following Presley's shock death at 27 of a suspected overdose.
Both he and Crawford were seen leaving the property together on Monday, the day after Presley died at an upscale rehab facility in the high-end neighborhood of Santa Monica, California.
Gerber's latest visit comes amid news that Presley has been cremated, according to a death certificate obtained by TMZ .
Presley was cremated at the Rose Family Funeral Home, with his occupation being described as an entrepreneur who worked in mental health.
Crawford and Gerber will reportedly keep their son's ashes at their Malibu home.
While an autopsy has been completed, the cause of death is currently pending investigation as the medical examiner waits for test results, per the outlet.
Sources told TMZ that the family is planning funeral arrangements, and the ceremony will be small.
Loved ones are said to be looking at both Forest Lawn or Malibu Presbyterian Church to hold the funeral within a week.

The family has been supported by close friends since the news of Presley's tragic passing, including actress Laura Dern and George Clooney.
New details about the circumstances in which Presley's body was discovered after his heartbreaking death reportedly came into focus this week.
On Wednesday, sources described as being close to the investigation said Presley had allegedly been found in a bedroom at the high-end rehab house on September 20, according to TMZ.
Presley had checked into the facility just the night before he was found dead after going into cardiac arrest .
According to TMZ, the sources with knowledge of the investigation alleged that Presley's body was not on the bed, but instead was found nearby in the room, though they did not specify an exact location.
The sources additionally told the publication that the potentially deadly narcotic fentanyl has not been a focus of the investigation into Presley's death at this time.
However, final confirmation of any substances that may have played a role in his death will have to wait until the Medical Examiner's toxicology report is released.
The Daily Mail previously obtained audio of the 911 emergency dispatch call made from the Santa Monica rehab, in which an automated voice could be heard saying 'cardiac arrest' followed by ‘overdose.'
The family is said to be planning funeral arrangements, and the ceremony will be small. Above, Gerber and Crawford with Presley and their daughter Kaia in 2018
The couple are said to be in total shock and devastated by the loss of their son. Above, the family in 2008
Presley was deeply loved and supported by his parents
Perhaps the most chilling detail from the 911 dispatch audio is how rapidly Presley's condition worsened within minutes.
The first call was made on Sunday, September 20, at 9.35am regarding a cardiac arrest; however, just three minutes later it was upgraded to an 'overdose,' then, at 9.40am the priority was upped once again as it was 'upgraded.'
Shortly after the release of the 911 dispatch audio, sources close to the model told TMZ on Tuesday that a physician had been prescribing him ketamine despite knowing his past problems with the drug.
Ketamine can be used to treat drug addiction ; however, that is not the use approved by the FDA.
Presley's close friends are allegedly angry that the doctor had prescribed the dissociative anesthetic to him while knowing that addiction struggles had been a regular problem for him, according to TMZ.
Over the past weekend on Sunday, it was announced that Presley had died following a years-long struggle with drugs, panic attacks and his mental health .
A Santa Monica Police Department spokesperson confirmed to The Daily Mail on Monday that emergency services were called to a luxury rehab Presley had been staying in on Sunday morning – before he was pronounced dead at the scene.
Per TMZ, Presley had been staying in a separate house on the grounds of the LA rehab, and had roommates. It was also claimed Presley had only checked into the rehab on Saturday night, hours before his death.

The model had been open about his decade-long struggle with drug addiction and mental health struggles.
Earlier this year, he posted about having a 'Pre-ibogaine flood dose' at a Mexican treatment clinic, a single, high-dose administration of the naturally occurring psychoactive substance ibogaine.
Ibogaine is derived from an African shrub and is reported to help with withdrawal symptoms. The high dose is designed to induce a profound 'reset.'
Presley's parents and his sister Kaia, 25, praised him for his 'courage' in response to his post about starting the treatment in March.
Crawford commented: 'You are a warrior! Walked thru the fire to find yourself! So proud!' while Kaia added: 'That's my brother I am so damn proud.'
And his father wrote: 'I'm so proud of you and your courage. Facing what's hard takes real strength and watching you find your way back to yourself is everything. I love you so much.’
Last November, Presley revealed he had taken a step back from social media to 'take care of my own mental health for a bit.'
One month later, he opened up about his personal life in a candid social media video. He started sharing 'Mental Health Mondays' videos on his Instagram. In one, he listed the medication he takes for 'night terrors' and 'panic attacks.'
Kaia praised her brother's willingness to strip away the secrecy surrounding his struggles. Above, Kaia and Presley in 2017
The tragedy cuts short the life of a model who had seemingly been destined to follow his famous mother into fashion from an early age.
Presley started modeling at age 15 and was featured in campaigns for fashion labels such as Dolce & Gabbana and Calvin Klein.
Presley was signed to IMG Models and appeared in a 2018 Pepsi ad with his mother.

articles.title_orig: China, US agree to AI dialogue, tariff cuts on $30 billion in goods during Xi visit
articles.title_zh: China, US agree to AI dialogue, tariff cuts on $30 billion in goods during Xi visit
articles.content_orig:
China and the United States agreed to establish a channel for handling AI-related incidents and accelerate work on military crisis communications following a three-day summit between President Xi Jinping and President Trump in Washington, the two governments said Saturday.
They also agreed to continue cooperating through a Board of Trade focused on selected bilateral issues. The White House said the board began operating this week.
The summit produced no major breakthroughs, but analysts said the steps toward greater cooperation were important because they established working groups that could help prevent disputes from escalating.
Xi returned to Beijing on Saturday, according to the state-run Xinhua News Agency. During the visit, Mr. Trump displayed unusual warmth toward Xi, despite having escalated a trade war with China the previous year that had global repercussions.
The two sides agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding on strengthening crisis communications and preventing crises between the two militaries, China's Foreign Ministry said Saturday in its readout. The one-page statement from the Chinese side was light on details.
Both sides will set up a communication mechanism for artificial intelligence-related incidents, to discuss related risks and benefits, with an AI-specific dialogue scheduled for November.
The White House said the two leaders agreed on using the term "super intelligence" rather than "artificial intelligence" to describe the technology. Mr. Trump has been outspoken about his preference for the alternate term.
"I call it SI because it's a much better name," he told reporters Saturday on the White House's south lawn. "It's a much more accurate name because when you say the other, it means it's fake. Artificial means it's fake, and it's not fake."
Mr. Trump also indicated that there would be limits on what the U.S. would share with China and said that Washington would not slow its AI efforts .
The "United States of America is not going to be putting on brakes," Mr. Trump told reporters outside the White House. "They want to stop our progress because we're leading China by a lot and we're going to keep it that way."
He added: "I would rather not integrate because we're leading by a lot. When you're leading, you don't open it up to each other. We're leading by at least a year, maybe a year and a half. Some people say two years. I'm not looking to open it up."
The statement from China said both sides will continue to work together on the pledge to reduce reciprocal tariffs on roughly $30 billion worth of goods. During the summit, the two leaders agreed to extend a trade truce by two months. The White House statement said China agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the U.S. in 2027 and 2028.
Most of the reduction in tariffs is aimed at non-sensitive goods, such as agricultural products or holiday decorations.
The two countries also established the Board of Investment to "discuss potential investment opportunities and investment-related impediments and to provide a structured channel for the two sides to address commercially meaningful investment-related issues," the White House said.
The statement from the White House also said the two sides continued to work on American concerns about rare earths supply , "with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels." China put export controls on rare earths last year in response to the U.S. tariffs, cutting the supply sent to the U.S. and other countries.
Both sides agreed to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, and then later at the G20 at the Trump National Doral Miami golf club in Florida.
Both governments said Iran should honor its stated commitment not to develop nuclear weapons. They also said no country should charge tolls on international waterways, an apparent reference to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has fallen significantly since the U.S. war with Iran began.
The U.S. statement welcomed China's decision to impose export controls on two additional precursor chemicals used to produce fentanyl. Both sides also noted recent arrests in fentanyl-related cases.
Although the summit did not resolve the countries' fundamental differences, analysts said the incremental progress was noteworthy.
"Personal diplomacy between the two leaders is important, but the emphasis on working-level engagement, military-to-military dialogue and crisis-management mechanisms suggests an effort to make that stability more durable and institutionalized," said Wang Zichen, deputy secretary-general of the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization.

articles.title_orig: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day roadmap to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump has rejected a roadmap submitted by Iran to open the Strait of Hormuz within a week.
“I reject their proposal,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday, adding that Iran wants an agreement because they’re “losing so badly”.
“They want to make a deal and I think that’s fine,” he said. “I’d like to make a deal, too. But that deal would not be acceptable.”
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday that Tehran formally submitted a seven-day roadmap to the US via mediator Qatar, and was awaiting Washington’s response.
“It appears as though the proposal is dead in the water,” said Al Jazeera’s Mike Hanna, reporting from Washington, DC.
Late on Friday, US media reports indicated Trump would reject the proposal .
Trump was “privately sceptical” that Tehran would meet his demands, and reportedly told aides that he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the November US midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, quoting unnamed US officials.
“President Trump has vacillated between extreme optimism, saying that ‘talks are going well’ to ‘I want to annihilate Iran’,” Hanna said about the recent diplomacy between Washington and Tehran.
“There is no consistency in terms of the [Trump] administration’s reaction,” he said.
But “the one thing that has been made clear by President Trump is that he is content to stay in the status of limbo”, Hanna added, despite concerns from much of the American public that the Iran conflict is turning into another “never-ending war”.
The Strait of Hormuz, a waterway key to the world’s oil supply, is central to the conflict between the US and Iran, which is at an impasse after nearly seven months, though new mediation efforts took place this week.
Earlier in the week, Araghchi held talks with Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital shipping channel.
On Friday, the top Iranian diplomat said: “Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days.”
He was speaking at the United Nations in New York, where he and other senior Iranian officials were attending the General Assembly.
Under the plan, Washington would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observe a ceasefire covering the region, including Lebanon and Yemen.
“The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure,” Araghchi had said.
On Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera that Tehran no longer trusts negotiations with the US after previous rounds of talks were followed by attacks and sanctions.
“We have no trust in the American side and do not know on what basis an understanding can be reached with it,” said Pezeshkian, who was also in New York for the UNGA.
He denied that Iran was responsible for blocking the Strait of Hormuz, saying the US “closed the routes before us”. He described the closure as “a natural response when routes are cut off to Iran”.
The Iranian president said the crisis could be resolved through negotiations rather than force, and that the waterway would reopen to commercial shipping if talks ended the war.

articles.title_orig: Third person arrested in death of Tasia Fortune, as police say hanging was staged
articles.title_zh: Third person arrested in death of Tasia Fortune, as police say hanging was staged
articles.content_orig:
Warning: This story contains distressing details
Police in the US state of Mississippi have said they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" by being placed hanging in a tree.
The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.
The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.
The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.
Police said that the medical examiner had determined that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".
Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging may have been staged.
Fortune's mother told the BBC that she remembered the coroner telling her: "We're not treating this as [an] actual hanging." Her daughter, they told her, was dead before being placed in the tree.
Christy Spivey also recalled police telling her the incident was "drug related".
She described how she knew her daughter fought for her life till the very end while speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday.
"I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey said, adding that Fortune had left behind four young children, aged seven, five, four and one.
Dressed in a shirt that read "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she did not want to see any innocent people going to jail.
"I just hope they have the right people," she said.
Three people have so far been arrested in relation to the case, all of whom are black, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody without bail.
A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in relation to the case this week.
A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.
The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.
Representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, cited at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress , external , which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.
The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has since been ruled a suicide.

articles.title_orig: 4 American tourists dead after building explosion and collapse in Athens
articles.title_zh: 4 American tourists dead after building explosion and collapse in Athens
articles.content_orig:
The building in the Plaka district was reduced to rubble strewn with household items
Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.
Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building.
Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.
All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, news agency Reuters reported citing local police.
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Investigators at the scene believe the blast was caused by a gas leak
Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are aware of a suspected explosion in Athens and are in touch with the local authorities."

articles.title_zh: Nor'easter storm brings coastal flooding, as New York and New Jersey declare emergency
articles.content_orig:
Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities flooded
Tens of millions of people across the north-eastern US are in the path of a powerful storm this weekend, which has already brought coastal flooding, power outages, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.
Peaking on Saturday, the so-called nor'easter will "bring dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds, and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said.
States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, the latter of which is already facing a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds are forecast from Virginia to Maine.
Ed Sheeran's much-awaited Boston concert was among events called off.
Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhood
The nor'easter is already causing widespread power outages. Nearly 150,000 households have so far lost electricity, according to poweroutageus.
The Federal Aviation Administration recommended flyers check with airlines about their flight status. More than 1,100 flights have been delayed and another 400 grounded, according to FlightAware.

articles.title_zh: White House Blocks CNN From Air Force One, Networks Suspend Pool Coverage Again
articles.content_orig:
CNN had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One
Broadcaster CNN has been barred from travelling with US President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday.
The move is the latest in a battle between the White House and the media after it was forced to lift its ban on some news outlets.
CNN was scheduled to fly with Trump for his trip to Tennessee for a college American football game until a note released on Friday night by the White House did not list the broadcaster on the media schedule.
The BBC has requested comment from the White House.
CNN has reported that no other outlet was listed as replacing them in the president's tentative schedule.
Last week, Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists from the White House after accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.
All three media outlets said they were pursuing legal action and accused Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.
Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage alongside CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets.
The White House then launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York.
A federal judge has since ruled that Trump barring news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional and that the administration had to let them back in, at least for now.
However, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals at a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.
In a series of online posts on Saturday, Trump criticised the CNN and other media outlets dubbing them "fake news".
"FAKE NEWS SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED IN THE WHITE HOUSE," he said.
A White House communications account earlier posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event and every press call".
Regular US television coverage resumed on Friday after White House officials allowed reporters entry.
The president is set to attend a football game between University of Tennessee vs University of Texas College at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville from midday local time on Saturday.

articles.title_orig: How Long Does The New Siri AI Take To Activate On iOS 27?
articles.title_zh: How Long Does The New Siri AI Take To Activate On iOS 27?
articles.content_orig:
Apple released its new iOS 27 update in September 2026, and users have been taking advantage of new features like AI photo-editing capabilities and child safety tools. One of the top headline features, though, is the newly-revamped Siri AI. But even if you have a compatible iPhone , you need  to request access from Apple to actually get Siri AI enabled , as it's still technically in testing. When you do, Apple says you'll be waitlist waitlisted, but it's unclear for how long.
Technically speaking, Apple says Siri AI is still in its beta phase despite the deep integration of AI into iOS 27 , so some people may wait longer than others. However, if you want to check for yourself, you can navigate to Settings > Siri and then tap Try Siri AI (Beta) to see if it's enabled or join the waitlist. You may need to enable Siri before completing this step.
Apple users who have received access have posted online that they spent anywhere from a couple of hours to several weeks on the waitlist. Communities on Reddit and longtime Apple watchers suspect the company may be releasing the AI in stages, to help with server load during this transition and roll out. Other AI providers have also reported significant demand when they release new products.
Looking at the r/iOS27 and r/Apple subreddits, people have stated different times for when they received access to the new Siri AI. Some have said they waited over 24 hours for Siri to arrive, while it took up to 48 hours for others. It's also worth noting that Siri AI is currently only available in English, as support for languages like Spanish, Korean, Japanese, Portuguese and French should begin rolling out in October 2026.
If you see a banner in Settings stating "Optimizing Search and Siri," this means your iPhone is still pouring through your device's storage to rebuild your search index, which is like a table of contents. It's likely one reason why one user within the Community forums on Apple's website reported waiting six days to receive access. Additionally, one user in the r/iOS27 subreddit mentions speaking to Apple about the issue, though the representative apparently said they cannot access the Siri AI waitlist, nor provide additional information.
For those who have been waiting for the update, having to wait a little longer can certainly be frustrating. In previous years, some users have even sued the company over its Siri marketing, reaching a settlement in which the company is paying $95 each to many iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 users .
While some people online have expressed frustration over the wait, not everyone feels that way. As one user on the r/Apple subreddit said, "You also waited a year for iOS 27 to come out, what's another day or two?"

articles.title_orig: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
articles.title_zh: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
articles.content_orig:
An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.
The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.
It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.
The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.
Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.
University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report - published by UVU - says.
"But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds.
Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.
They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team.
A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said.
The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures.
However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.
Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice , a step that can precede legal action.
The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones.
"The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."
When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.
The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events.
UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".
It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures that are common practice at US high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.
Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.
His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

articles.title_orig: Rogue OpenAI agents targeted three separate US government websites
articles.title_zh: Rogue OpenAI agents targeted three separate US government websites
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI said Friday that some of its AI agents went rogue and probed US government websites this summer — the latest revelation of the artificial intelligence company’s technology.
The New York Times first reported that the AI agents went rogue and attempted to gain access to the Education Department, the Commerce Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission, according to security researchers at AI research lab Transluce.
OpenAI said Saturday that its agents accessed publicly available data from the Commerce Department’s Census Bureau using login credentials it found online, and separately shared public data from the SEC website on another website. OpenAI’s agents attempted but failed to gain access to the Education Department and gather data from its civil rights office, according to the report.
OpenAI told CNN in an email that it notified the agencies of the findings while continuing an “extensive review of misaligned model activity.”
“Most of the activity we’ve reviewed so far involved routine research tasks, such as accessing public web content to answer questions. Some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information,” the spokesperson said.
The Commerce Department, SEC and Education Department did not immediately respond to CNN’s requests for comment.
Rep. Jay Obernolte, the Republican co-chair of the AI caucus, told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Friday that the incident is “another example of a loss of human control.”
“We need to align the values that these models are trained on with human values, and if we can do that, we can get these models to conform to our standards for human behavior,” he said.
The report comes just days after Australia’s prime minister said that an OpenAI agent hacked into the country’s national healthcare database, marking the first known case of AI hacking a government network. Transluce on Wednesday said that it had detected AI agents going rogue dating back to at least March, unsuccessfully targeting a University of New Mexico library and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare site.
The Australian website probe occurred in June, an OpenAI spokesperson previously told CNN, but the company was only made aware of it in August.
OpenAI has been investigating agents’ use of internet access since the breach of AI start-up Hugging Face in July.
Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, said Friday on social media site X that the company was not “as fast as we would have liked.”
“We are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding … Hugging Face is still the most severe event we’ve seen,” he wrote .
Competitors Anthropic , Meta and Google have also reported that their agents have gone rogue during breach attempts.
Such breaches have raised alarms within the artificial intelligence community. Tech leaders have jointly called for a slowdown of the technology’s development following Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s essay about “ pacing the frontier ” in mid-September. Amodei warned that people may lose control of AI, which could be misused for “cyberattacks and bioterrorism.”
During the United Nations’ General Assembly on Wednesday, Amodei and Altman urged the UN Security Council to set international standards. Altman said countries need accurate and speedy reporting so that the “world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes.”
Amodei’s warning followed a former Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, whose viral post on X called out AI companies for not acting responsibly with the technology’s development and warned that it “will kill us all.”
AI “doomerism” has faced pushback from tech leaders like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who said there’s a “0% chance” of the world coming to an end in 2030.
CNN’s Hadas Gold, Hilary Whiteman and Max Saltman contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress Literally Melts Off Her Body on Stage in a Moment of Fashion Magic
articles.title_zh: Olivia Rodrigo’s Dress Literally Melts Off Her Body on Stage in a Moment of Fashion Magic
articles.content_orig:
It’s official: Wounds are healing. Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled Tour last night in Hartford, Connecticut, with an opening-night triumph that proved she might be feeling unraveled, but totally unvanquished. What a night — O-Rod held the stage for nearly two hours, going on at 8 p.m. sharp to storm through 23 songs, without an encore or a dull moment. She did nearly every song from her new You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love — it was a barrage of one killer tune after another, from her three already-classic albums. Flowers. Rain. A dissolving dress. Now that’s a rock star — it’s the most alive she’s ever been.
It’s a totally bonkers show — the whole night is full of her Fuck It, Whatever energy. The stage is covered with flowers. Tons of flowers. So many flowers. Olivia has to be the only pop star I’ve seen with her own flower roadies — by my count there were 16 people in the gardening crew, coming out between songs to gather or rearrange the foliage, or else to bring more. You have never beheld so much vegetation onstage. Guess Olivia really does have a favorite florist?
The Unraveled Tour is a world away from the brazen glam-punk bravado of her summer-2025 festival run, barely a year ago, where she kicked off every night with the grunge headbanger “Obsessed” — a song she hasn’t touched all year. In that show, she was absolutely on top of the world, lit up with superhuman rock confidence. She’s in different territory emotionally these days, going for a pastoral mood. After Wolf Alice’s high-energy opening set, her pre-show soundtrack was a loop of chirping insects and birds.
Olivia made an unforgettable surprise entrance — the band stretched out the intro to “ Drop Dead ” forever, until Olivia sang the first verse while entirely hidden in the flowers. For the first chorus — “One night I was bored in bed” — she arose from deep in the garden, like a May Queen. Before long, the guitars were blasting away while purple confetti fell. She rocked out in a white dress with an empire silhouette, giving total Pride and Prejudice vibes, if there were a sixth Bennet sister who hung out in pubs and knew all the words to “Just Like Heaven.”
Quite honestly, Olivia could have left the stage after “Drop Dead” and it would have been a fantastic show. But she was just starting, slamming right into two of the greatest (and rockingest) love songs she’s ever written, “U + Me = <3” and “So American.” “U + Me” was lifted high by the crowd screaming the key lines, maybe Olivia’s all-time killer couplet if not her entire philosophy of life: “They say modern love’s a cruel endeavor/And to that I say fuck it, whatever!” The video screen helpfully displayed the lyrics, but nobody needed a prompt. She raced to the keyboard to play a piano solo. At one point, she lifted her dress to show the crowd her underwear, decorated with a pro-Hartford message: “HFD + me 4ever.” (Note: There is no known evidence of anyone ever feeling this way about Hartford in real life.)
“So American” was a shocker in the setlist — it seemed like a song she was guaranteed not to do, since it’s very much set in the pre- You Seem So Sad era, but it brilliantly raised the emotional stakes. The three-song interlude of romantic bliss hit a nasty snag with the pop-punk rage of “Good 4 U”; it led to a costume change while the band vamped on the “Deja Vu” intro and the flower roadies pruned the garden.
The show is grouped in six different sections, loosely ( very loosely) based around the four seasons. She kept the energy level high with her all-woman band, starring guitar heroes Daisy Spencer (whom she introduced as “the coolest girl in the world”) and Arianna Powell. There was hardly any stage banter, especially in the first half, where she rarely said a word between songs — she’s never talked so little in a show. Her outfits ranged from princess dresses to Nineties-style streetwear. The indie-sleaze aggro of “My Way” zipped right into the amazing new “Serena Joy,” a righteously pissed-off feminist broadside with a very early-Eighties new wave groove, very Martha and the Muffins. “Purple” began with Olivia curled up into a ball on the floor, by the lip of the stage, until she was jumping around waving a sparkler by the end. Related Content iHeartRadio’s 2026 Jingle Ball Tour Recruits Olivia Rodrigo, Hilary Duff, Sombr Olivia Rodrigo Is the Best Arena Rock Act in Years Watch Olivia Rodrigo Sing ‘Strong Enough’ for Sheryl Crow in Nashville Here's Who We Want to See at Daisy Chain 2027
You Seem Pretty Sad for a Girl So in Love is a highly plot-driven album (a plus or a minus, depending on your mindset or mood), but she avoids that narrative in the live show, taking care to switch back and forth between falling-in-love songs and break-up songs. “Cigarette Smoke” actually comes before “Honeybee,” which is a daring move since it reverses the album’s apiology imagery. But she didn’t say anything about the album’s much-discussed premise, staying away from any comments that might seem conceptual or thematic. The one new song that got an introduction was “Begged,” which she prefaced with a sweet story about writing it “in a hotel room in a foreign country at 4 a.m.,” while her best friend Madison Hu was trying to sleep. (She apologized to Hu, who was in the audience, saying, “Sorry, Maddie, for keeping you up.”)
She also led the crowd in a birthday tribute. “This is a special night, because it’s opening night,” she said at her piano. “But also because it’s my mom’s birthday.” Since her mom was there in the house, she had everyone sing “Happy Birthday,” but quipped, “I can’t put her on camera — she’d kill me!”
“Bad Idea Right?” and “Vampire” were highlights, with Olivia reprising her iconic Guts- era stage crawl during Powell’s guitar solo in the former. For “Stupid Song,” she moved to a heart-shaped side stage (with a ring of flowers, of course). “Maggots for Brains,” one of the weirdest, saddest, and best moments on the new album, killed, with Olivia playing the Cure-style guitar solo. (Robert Smith did not show up tonight, and sadly, neither did “What’s Wrong With Me,” the only omission from You Seem Pretty Sad ). Olivia sat alone at the piano for the rapturously received “Favorite Crime” and “Drivers License.”
The show climaxed with the one-two punch of “Deja Vu” and “All-American Bitch,” two of her toughest ragers. The set omitted some of her bad-attitude rockers like “Brutal,” “Obsessed,” or “Get Him Back!,” any of which might have added some spice to the ending, since “Expectations” doesn’t quite have the knockout punch for a finale; at least a few people in my section began singing “Brutal” before realizing this was a different song with a similar beat. Peter Gabriel Confronts Death on New Song 'Face the Wall' ‘Heart of the Beast’ Feels Like Something Brad Pitt Made 30 Years Ago
But the night’s killer moment came during “The Cure,” the most gloriously heartbreaking song she’s ever written, and the emotional center of this show as well as the album. Olivia moved to a center stage to deliver her vulnerable confessions of insecurity and self-doubt. But an unseen cloud over her head began to rain on her — actual water, soaking her through — until the rain washed away her dress. She stood alone, unraveled, as her dress dissolved along with her emotional defenses. It was an over-the-top moment that suited the emotional power of the song as well as this entire night.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Saturday (September 26, 2026) announced a slew of measures addressing concerns over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls across the country, including stopping physical hearings for unmapped voters or those with logical discrepancies in their enumeration forms.
It said that the declaration accompanying Form 6 (used for fresh voter registration) is mandatory only during the current SIR process. This in effect means that new voters who seek inclusion in electoral rolls after the ongoing SIR need not submit any such declaration.
The commission also said that any person whose name has got left out during SIR or thereafter, and any person including young/ first-time voters, may apply to the electoral registration officer (ERO) concerned, for inclusion of their names in the electoral rolls.  A special drive will immediately be launched for their enrolment, it said in a press note.
The SIR process has already been completed in 20 States and Union Territories.
The fresh initiatives of the poll body came after a meeting of the full bench of the commission on Saturday afternoon (September 26, 2026) and days after reports emerged of a rift within the Election Commissioners over these and other issues in the SIR process as well as the internal working of the ECI.
The press note confirmed that the two Commissioners had written to the Cabinet Secretary but said it was not related to any policy matter of the commission or IT division but related to working of an officer on deputation to the ECI. “The work re-distribution orders issued by the concerned officer were not actually implemented after the orders of the two Commissioners,” it clarified.
The commission’s press note was pertinently accompanied by a photograph of all the three Election Commissioners and mentioned that it “has the approval of the full commission”.
As far as physical hearings were concerned, the statement said: “In case of any person to whom notice has been issued during the ongoing SIR, for being unmapped and for logical discrepancies, BLOs (booth-level officers) will visit the homes of such persons for collection of documents and thereafter upload them on the ECINet, for decision by the ERO.”
“Such persons need not be called for hearing to ERO/AERO office. Only in exceptional circumstances, as decided by the ERO, the hearing will be held preferably online. Any adult member of the family can be authorised by the elector to attend the hearing on their behalf, if required. Facilities for the online hearing are to be strengthened.”
As regards new voter registration, the EC maintained that the declaration form attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Supreme Court, but for non-SIR period, the forms appFmahalicable as per rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used for new voter inclusion.
Also read | Declaration part of Form 6 changed since SIR in Bihar
The other issue that had attracted the ire of the two Election Commissioners was the supposed centralisation of management of voter rolls through the ECINet portal, with field officers unable to access it in many cases.
The statement said that “A Committee headed by Sr. Deputy Election Commissioner (DEC) and including an independent expert from IIT/IIIT will review the ECINET to double-check that it complies with the provisions of the Acts and Rules and submit report to the Commission”. It added that henceforth, all the new initiatives about IT modules and portals will be discussed in the Committee of Officers (COO) before approval by the commission.
“Field officers have role-based access to the ECINET system as per their statutory powers. In case, any further flexibility is required by the field officers, that will be made operational,” it added.
The commission also extended the period for filing claims and objections for Delhi till October 30 and for Maharashtra till October 12.
Many other administrative measures were also announced. These include circulation of an advanced agenda and issuance of minutes for all of Commission’s meetings, completion of annual performance appraisal reports of all the officers within the stipulated time frame, approval of the commission for foreign trips of officers and compliance with all directions issued by the Commissioners to the officers of the Commission.
The Opposition, which has been seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, remained unimpressed with the statement. Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said: “The CEC thinks he can hide behind protocol. He stands exposed and is now petrified as an entire country seeks to hold him accountable.”

articles.title_zh: The 10-year Treasury yield is at its highest in nearly two decades. How we got here
articles.content_orig:
Investors were rattled this week as the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield soared to its highest level since 2007, but sticky inflation is just one of the factors behind this latest surge.
The key 10-year Treasury yield , which influences mortgages, leapt to 5.23% on Friday for its highest level since 2007. It was the latest leg higher for the benchmark yield, which earlier this month was trading just below 4.8%. Bond yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The 10-year yield's rapid climb above 5% shows how quickly investors' expectations have shifted toward additional tightening from the Federal Reserve in light of stubborn inflation. Fed funds futures trading shows a 64% likelihood of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool.
Indeed, the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index showed that year-ahead inflation expectations leapt to 4.6% in September, rising from 4% in August and marking the highest reading since June.
When it comes to the runup in yields, stubborn inflation and the market's growing anticipation for more rate hikes only tell part of the story, according to Thierry Wizman, global FX and rates strategist at Macquarie Group.
"I think this year it has more to do with the bond issuance than the inflation story," he told CNBC.
Wizman said yields at these levels are not themselves unusual, particularly because they are not being accompanied by extreme inflation expectations or an aggressively tightening Fed.
"We don't have a Federal Reserve that's tightening aggressively, so a lot of things look pretty normal. The thing that's abnormal is that we're in the midst of a very strong investment cycle," he said.
The federal government is issuing debt to finance a large deficit, while companies are borrowing heavily to fund artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Wizman said it is that combination that has increased bond supply enough to put upward pressure on yields.
The AI spending boom is adding another source of bond supply to compete with Treasuries.
Vanguard estimates that Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft and Oracle issued about $132 billion of debt through July, up sharply from the roughly $35 billion annual average between 2020 and 2024. Broader AI-related debt issuance could reach $300 billion to $570 billion this year as companies across the data-center, semiconductor and utility ecosystem borrow to finance the buildout.
At the same time, higher yields can weigh down stocks by raising borrowing costs for companies and making bonds seem more attractive to income-seeking investors.
Wizman said the capital-spending plans of hyperscalers and their suppliers are likely to keep bond issuance elevated through this year and into next year.
"So these yields could go higher," he said.

Sylvester Stallone told Fox News Digital he is still happy with his choice to permanently relocate to Florida from Hollywood last year.
Sylvester Stallone isn't looking for pity.
The action star opened up about a childhood marked by abandonment, violence and an almost total absence of affection in a new interview, telling The New York Times that he deliberately left some of the darkest stories out of his book because he didn't want readers to feel sorry for him.
"I didn't put a lot of stuff in the book because I didn't want a pity party … but it was insane," he admitted.
SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS WHAT HE SAID TO TRUMP AFTER SURPRISE HOLLYWOOD AMBASSADOR APPOINTMENT
Sylvester Stallone reflects on his abusive childhood ahead of the release of his memoir, "The Steps." (Getty Images)
After his parent’s divorce, Stallone spent time living with his father in Maryland. He described his father as volatile and physically abusive.
"The next thing you know — wham! He had very big hands. You just learned to duck a little bit."
One memory particularly stayed with Stallone.
The Hollywood star said his father sent him to a store before church to buy bread. He returned with nut bread after running into friends.
"And he kicked me in the stomach and hit me and like laid me out, got in the car, and went to church."
Stallone said he was left lying in the street, saying, "Really, it's unbelievable. It's unbelievable."
Years later, Stallone confronted his father. When he was in his 40s, Stallone told him, "I wish you and I could be the same age for three minutes." When his father asked him why, he said, "Because I'd like to give you some of your own medicine, and you would know what it'd be like to have your ass kicked."
Stallone said his father then challenged him to fight, explaining, "He was ready to go at 68 years old."
Sylvester Stallone is seen in "Rambo: First Blood Part II." (Nancy Moran/Sygma)
The "Rocky" star connected that fierceness to the one of the characters he's best known for.
"So, when people go, ‘Where do you get the ferocity to play Rambo?' Genetic," he said.
Stallone additionally recalled that his mother never showed affection towards him.
SYLVESTER STALLONE'S 'TULSA KING' SEASON 4 TEASER SPARKS FAN FRENZY: 'THE KING IS BACK!'
"My mother never — and my brother will attest — hugged me. Ever, ever," Stallone shared.
His father rarely showed affection either. But when Stallone was about 9, he said he fell asleep in the car after working around his father's horses. His father placed Stallone's head on his knee and rested his hand on his head.
"And I never got over that," he admitted.
Sylvester Stallone, best known for playing Rocky Balboa, is opening up about the abusive childhood that shaped his life. (Getty Images)

Earlier in the interview, Stallone described being sent to live in a boarding house when he was very young, where his parents visited only once a month.
"I just was raised by strangers, you know, in a boarding house. And it became sort of a natural environment. And my parents were really never nurturing, so this was actually a bonus compared to where I was living."
That emotional deprivation, Stallone acknowledged, shaped the man he became.
When asked whether it made him tough, he replied, "In the wrong way, yeah, it did. It made me very tough."
Sylvester Stallone, seen with wife Jennifer Flavin, credited his family with giving him the stability he lacked growing up. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images)
But the toughness came at a cost. Stallone said he didn't experience what he considers "real, real, real, real true love" until he was around 70, when he experienced it with his wife and kids, saying, "And that's a big pity. It really is."

Stallone went on to build one of Hollywood's most recognizable careers, writing and starring as Rocky Balboa and going on to play John Rambo. The original "Rocky" received 10 Oscar nominations and won three Academy Awards , including best picture.
Off-screen, Stallone has five children from two of his three marriages.

articles.title_orig: Trump revives rare budget maneuver to rescind $810M in congressionally approved funds
articles.title_zh: Trump revives rare budget maneuver to rescind $810M in congressionally approved funds
articles.content_orig:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
The Trump administration announced Friday that it was canceling $810 million in congressionally approved spending for programs serving illegal immigrants, diversity initiatives and other efforts the administration argued do not benefit American citizens.
To claw back the funds, President Donald Trump used a "pocket rescission," a budget maneuver the executive branch contends is within its authority but that Congress and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) say exceeds the president's authority.
The vast majority of the cuts, some $567 million, were aimed at Health and Human Services programs that provided funding to non-government organizations supporting refugees, asylees and other non-citizens .
The White House is also seeking to rescind $25 million for education programs for migrant students, claiming they supported things such as "an LGBT youth summit" and "Therapy for Latinx workshops."
FILE - The majority of the cuts were aimed at Health and Human Services programs. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
TRUMP ADMIN AXES TIES TO DOZENS OF PROGRESSIVE GROUPS IN 'DIRECT OPPOSITION' TO MISSION: 'DECISIVE ACTION'
Programs the administration labeled "Woke International Education" were also selected for $70 million in cuts. The White House said the funding supports bringing foreign students and faculty to the United States and, in some cases, has funded doctoral dissertations on "queer and trans community building in foreign countries."
Other programs receiving the axe included a Justice Department office focused on reducing racial tensions, a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs, Housing and Urban Development Department counseling services, and a series of Health and Human Services grants the administration described as "outright harmful and blatantly ideological."
The White House's announcement about the rescissions noted that several of the organizations are led by former officials in President Barack Obama's administration.
Sen. Susan Collins , R-Maine, who faces a tough re-election campaign, condemned Trump's cuts and called it "the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse."
FILE - Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, accused the Trump administration of undermining Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse. (CJ Gunther/Getty Images)
WHITE HOUSE LAUNCHES INTERACTIVE MAP TRACKING BILLIONS IN SUSPECTED FRAUD
Under the most recent pocket rescission, the White House proposed canceling the funding near the end of the federal fiscal year on Sept. 30.
Collins argued that this was intentional on the part of the Trump administration, because if the money remains unspent until Sept. 30, it expires before Congress' 45-day review period can be completed.
On top of that, the House of Representatives will be out of session through the November election, making it essentially impossible for Congress to respond.
"The independent Government Accountability Office has concluded that pocket rescissions are unlawful and not permitted by the Impoundment Control Act," Collins said in a statement. "I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions."
FILE - Russell Vought, director of the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), said the Impoundment Control Act does not forbid the president from rescinding funds near the end of a fiscal year. (Jason Andrew/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The OMB under Trump has argued that the Impoundment Control Act does not explicitly forbid the president from rescinding funds near the end of a fiscal year, according to a summary from the Congressional Research Service (CRS) . OMB Director Russ Vought has repeatedly said the same.
That same CRS summary said the GAO has likened pocket rescissions to a line-item veto, which would allow a president to strike portions of legislation without congressional approval — a power the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional.
A year ago, Trump issued the first pocket rescission in nearly 50 years, seeking to cancel $4.9 billion in congressionally approved foreign aid. The Supreme Court declined to block the move, citing the president's authority over foreign affairs as it allowed litigation to continue.
The last pocket rescission took place under former President Jimmy Carter, who proposed it well before the 45-day congressional review deadline.

articles.title_orig: She grew up under Soviet rule. Now EU's top diplomat warns Europe against giving Russia what it wants
articles.title_zh: She grew up under Soviet rule. Now EU's top diplomat warns Europe against giving Russia what it wants
articles.content_orig:
In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, Vice-President of the European Commission Kaja Kallas discusses Iran diplomacy, Russian sabotage across Europe, and why she believes greater pressure is needed to bring Moscow to the negotiating table.
NEW YORK — Russia is trying to scare Europe into backing off its defense in the region, claims European Union’s top diplomat Kaja Kallas, who warns it will only lead to Moscow becoming more aggressive if it succeeds.
"Their goal is to intimidate us from not supporting Ukraine, from refraining to support them and pressuring Russia," Kallas told Fox News Digital in an interview on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
"What is important for us is that we are not afraid," she continued. "Because otherwise this kind of intimidation actually pays off, and then we will see more of it across the world."
For Kallas, Russia’s attempts to intimidate its European neighbors carry a history that reaches well beyond the war in Ukraine.
Kaja Kallas says Russia is trying to frighten Europe into backing away from Ukraine, a strategy the European Union’s top diplomat warns will only become more aggressive if it succeeds. (Fox News Digital)
Her mother, Kristi, was just six months old in 1949 when Soviet authorities deported her — along with her mother and her grandmother — to Siberia during Stalin’s mass deportations from the Baltic states. Kallas’ maternal grandfather was separately sent to a Siberian prison camp.
Kallas has recounted how her mother was transported east in a cattle car, with fellow deportees drying the infant’s diapers against their own bodies during the freezing journey. The family spent roughly a decade in Siberia before they were allowed to return to Soviet-occupied Estonia in 1959.
Kallas was born in Tallinn in 1977 and spent the first 14 years of her life under Soviet rule. Estonia restored its independence in 1991 as the Soviet Union collapsed.
FRONTLINE NATO ALLY SHARES SHOCKING TAKE ON RUSSIAN INVASION THREAT
Her family would go on to become deeply entwined with the new democratic Estonia. Her father, Siim Kallas, became the first president of the Bank of Estonia after gaining its independence, later serving as foreign minister and prime minister before moving to Brussels as a European commissioner.
Kaja Kallas followed her own path from lawyer to member of Estonia’s parliament and then the European Parliament.
In 2021, she became Estonia’s first female prime minister and three years later was chosen as the European Union’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy . It was a historic moment — putting a politician who grew up under Soviet occupation at the center of Europe’s response to Russian aggression on the continent.
That history has made Kallas one of Europe’s most prominent voices on Moscow — even as officials in her native Estonia and elsewhere along NATO’s eastern flank now caution against interpreting Russia’s recent provocations as preparations for a conventional invasion.
Russia invaded Ukraine more than four-and-a-half years ago and shows no signs of backing off despite repeated promises that negotiations for an end of war are ongoing.
Asked whether she agreed with Estonian and other Baltic officials who say they do not currently see Russia preparing for such an attack, Kallas instead pointed to Moscow’s growing use of sabotage and the importance of deterrence.
"We see that Russia is actually increasing their sabotage acts in Europe," Kallas said. "But of course how far they will go depends very much on us and whether we are investing enough in defense so that it acts as a deterrent."
The debate comes as NATO countries confront a string of Russian aircraft and drone incursions , along with suspected sabotage and other hybrid activity across Europe. The incidents have fueled warnings in some European capitals that Moscow is probing the alliance for weaknesses, while officials closer to Russia have cautioned against equating those provocations with preparations for an invasion.
US ALLIES NEED TO SHOOT DOWN RUSSIAN AIRCRAFT TESTING NATO BOUNDARIES, CZECH PRESIDENT WARNS
EU Commission vice-president, High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas (L) and the President of the European Commission Ursula von der Leyen (R) talk to the media. (Thierry Monasse/Getty Images)
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Fox News Digital in a separate interview this week that his country's intelligence services see no indication Russia is preparing for a full-scale attack on NATO.
"We have more and more this kind of panic in Europe that Russia will invade and will be full-scale aggressive against NATO and Europe and the Baltic states, Poland, but we don’t see it," Tsahkna said. "Our intelligence, we see very, very deep into Russia, we don’t see any change."
Kallas, however, argued that Moscow's actions are designed to weaken Western support for Ukraine rather than simply test NATO's defenses.
"Their goal is to intimidate us from not supporting Ukraine, from refraining to support them and pressuring Russia," she said.
The pressure campaign comes as Washington continues its push for a negotiated end to the war. Kallas said Moscow has yet to demonstrate that it is serious about reaching one.
"They should start with stopping bombing the civilians," she said, pointing to recent Russian attacks on Kyiv. "If they are serious about this, they should agree to a ceasefire, sit down at the negotiation table and talk to the Ukrainians."
The State Emergency Service put out a fire after a mass Russian drone and missile attack on the capital of Kyiv, July 4, 2025. ((Photo by Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images))
Kallas said Ukraine has already agreed to an unconditional ceasefire while "Russia is just playing games," arguing that coordinated pressure from Washington and its European allies could change Moscow's calculations.

"If America, Europe, UK, other strong players are all acting together in the same way to put in the sanctions, then actually we could have the effect that Russia understands that this is serious and they will sit down and negotiate," she said.

articles.title_orig: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.title_zh: Inside Meta's months-long grind to turn Muse into a hit
articles.content_orig:
A year ago, Meta was struggling to convince Silicon Valley that it could keep up in the AI race. Now it has one of the industry's hottest products.
Muse, Meta's new personal AI assistant, has rocketed to the top of the App Store and become a victory lap for CEO Mark Zuckerberg's massive AI spending. Meta's Connect conference this week was all about the app, which AI chief Alexandr Wang — who is 29 and has been posting risqué memes of Muse's mascot all week — called a "banger."
Getting there required months of painstaking work, a team led by former GitHub CEO Nat Friedman, and thousands of employees pulled from across Meta to teach the agent how to actually get things done, employees told Business Insider.
Meta also snapped up top AI agent talent through acqui-hires, including the leaders of Dreamer, an AI agent startup.
Whether Meta can sustain Muse's momentum is another question. Competitors like Instinct are thriving, and OpenAI is widely expected to launch a rival. Privacy concerns have also arisen, as Muse requires broad access to users' accounts to function. Meta employees are still reeling from a year of mass layoffs, employee surveillance, and low morale.
For now, at least, Muse's success — and a more than 20% increase in Meta's stock price since its launch — has become a morale boost, employees said. It also proves that Meta remains firmly in the AI race after being seen as a laggard a year ago.
"Muse is busy working for millions of people because of the hard work of a bunch of people at Meta — and we're still cooking," a Meta spokesperson said.
Muse's success was far from inevitable.
Since September 2025, Friedman, who heads the superintelligence unit's Products and Applied Research team , has been working hard on Muse, then codenamed "Hatch."
Take a smarter break in your day - and see how far you get.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
As recently as two weeks before Muse's launch this month, the chatbot struggled with speaking good English, a person directly familiar with the matter said — and it came as a huge relief when it finally started scoring well on coherence tests.
Earlier this year, some of Meta's top AI employees were also worried about Muse, an employee told Business Insider. They had tried it out and found it working poorly — it felt like just another chatbot, but with a worse underlying AI model and extra steps, that person added.
Friedman's team eventually pulled it off. Tens of thousands of Meta employees tested Muse for months, coming up with a range of use cases for the agent, which became key to the effort.
That data helped Friedman's team improve Muse's ability to do things like book meetings and cancel plane tickets: the painful work of getting better at increasingly complex tasks, or "hill-climbing," as Silicon Valley calls it.
The team trained Muse to be considerate so that it didn't overshare, like telling people someone couldn't make a meeting because they were hungover, the person familiar said. Meta also focused on ensuring it could interact with the internet seamlessly by using tools it hadn't used before.
"Our researchers did a ton of work teaching agents how to choose the right tool for a job," Wang said this week at Connect.
Friedman's role was critical. Zuckerberg brought in the executive last year as part of a deal to buy a stake in his venture capital fund, NFDG. Last year, Friedman and Wang cowrote a memo outlining a "superintelligent personal sidekick" that would act as a trusted friend and advisor.
Friedman is unabashedly technical and hands-on. Internally, the executive is opinionated and proud of it, chafing with other teams across Meta's sprawling operations, one of the employees said. Meta's communications chief, Andy Stone, recently called him "Nat the Truthteller" after he derided a report about Muse's security as written by "dummies."
He also moves fast. His bare-bones personal website spells out his philosophy in characteristically blunt terms: "slow is fake" and "it's important to do things fast," it says. Friedman has pushed Meta's AI staff to ditch slow internal tools in favor of faster external ones, such as Vercel.
When the independent AI agent OpenClaw took the tech world by storm this winter, Friedman acted quickly. The free desktop-based tool was popular with developers, but mystifying to everyday users. Friedman aimed to build a far more accessible version from scratch.
He issued a two-page internal memo titled "The Claw Is The Law," praising the product, and also bought hundreds of Mac Minis for Meta's superintelligence team to run the agent.
While Muse is user-friendly now, making it all happen took "months of blood, sweat, and tears," the person familiar said.
Although it took a "long ass time," now it's something that anyone's "grandma can use," Wang later posted.
Meta also went on a hiring binge for researchers and engineers in agentic AI. It hired David Singleton and Hugo Barra, the cofounders of Dreamer, a startup helping people build their own agents, along with the rest of their team.
Singleton has worked on Muse since he began at Meta in March, helping design the core technology that enables the app to store sensitive information securely, he posted on X.
The efforts worked. Although the arrival of the viral AI agent Instinct initially upstaged Meta , Muse took off by tapping into Meta's enormous built-in audience across its apps — including among people who had never used AI agents before.
Meta wasn't the only one on a hiring spree. OpenAI hired OpenClaw's creator , Pete Steinberger, in a coup earlier this year. Meta was especially worried that it would be upstaged by a large competitor, the person familiar with the matter said, and the team was shocked as the months went by without such an entrant.
Wall Street is cheering on Muse, seeing it as a way for Meta to become more than an ad company. Zuckerberg told Alex Heath's Sources earlier this month that he wants people to shop and save money on Muse, which Meta plans to make money from by taking a small cut of each transaction.
"We see the Meta bull case increasingly playing out," Mizuho Americas analyst Lloyd Walmsley wrote in a note.
Users have praised how easy it is to set up Muse. Hadi Javeed, the cofounder of healthcare startup RevelAi, said his dad saw an ad for Muse in his Facebook feed and downloaded it, promptly using it to buy a new pair of shoes.
"They completely deleted all the setup that was required," Javeed said.
At the same time, Javeed, like many others, has raised data privacy concerns about Muse. By design, an app like Muse creates a new order of security and privacy risks, such as the app buying things without a user's permission. Privacy and trust remain key roadblocks to broader adoption of Muse, Bank of America analysts wrote.
Zuckerberg has said that the company held back Muse's launch due to safety and product liability concerns. He and Friedman also personally reached out to Signal creator Moxie Marlinspike to help co-design Muse's security architecture, Zuckerberg told Heath.
For now, Meta is on a high. The company has hinted that much more will come as it works on a new AI model, Watermelon. It says the model has already caught up with OpenAI. Wang says Meta has other ideas that are "just as big" as Muse.
"The kitchen is just getting warmed up," he posted on X.

Indeed, the glasses were pretty much everywhere at the annual event, where Meta shows off its newest hardware and AI products. Both Meta staff and the flocks of influencers who frequent the event seemed to arrive with the glasses glued to their faces. Most of the demos the company offered this week also involved the glasses.
I swiftly joined the bespectacled masses and found myself trying on pair after pair of Meta’s high-tech specs.
One of the more notable products I had an opportunity to demo were Meta’s new, still-unreleased, audio-only smart glasses . News of these glasses emerged not long after the company weathered accusations that it was selling “pervert glasses,” with critics alleging that its camera-equipped specs could be used for nefarious surveillance purposes.
The new glasses come equipped with six microphones, but no camera, and they have no native way to record your surroundings, which should go a long way toward easing privacy concerns. They are significantly lighter than any of the other smart glasses I’ve worn, and they were quite comfortable.
The Meta staffer I talked to emphasized the glasses’ entertainment and communication options: You can listen to music easily (they’re more comfortable than earbuds) and take phone calls without reaching for your phone.
The glasses will also integrate with Muse, Meta’s personal agentic system, which can carry out tasks on the user’s behalf. The new integration, which isn’t yet available to the public, lets wearers speak to Muse and give it commands verbally. Meta also plans to personalize the agent, letting users pick from an assortment of cute digital avatars that can represent the agent when it communicates with them.
I was given an opportunity to try this out, which was fun but also somewhat comical. You have to be very direct with the agent, and you can’t talk to anyone else at the same time or it will get confused. Problematically, I kept chatting intermittently with the Meta staffer who’d given me the glasses, and the agent kept thinking I was speaking to it, so it would talk over her.
Still, in the right context, it’s easy to see how this new integration could be incredibly useful. If you don’t mind being seen in public talking to your own sunglasses, you’ll be able to ask Muse to take care of various digital tasks for you, like sending emails or reciting to-do lists, and it will handle them while you’re out grocery shopping or having a beer. You can also ask the glasses anything, and like a mobile version of ChatGPT, they’ll spit out an answer. (I asked the glasses a question about World War II, and they gave me a succinct and historically accurate response.)
Finally, I also got to test-drive a second audio-only pair: Meta’s new glasses for the hearing impaired. Given that hearing loss affects many families (some 50 million Americans are said to have some level of hearing loss), this device, unlike a lot of other modern tech gadgets, serves a clear and practical purpose.
I spoke briefly with a member of Meta’s research team who said the glasses had been in development for about five years, and he pointed out a price difference that could make them appealing: Whereas a lot of hearing aids can run as high as $1,600, the glasses will sell for $150.
The experience of wearing these glasses was interesting. Meta had me put earplugs in before trying them on to simulate the hearing loss that the glasses are meant to help users overcome. Once the glasses were on, they seemed to amplify the voice of the person I was talking to. Users can switch the amplification from focused, which zeroes in on the person in front of them, to omnidirectional, which picks up sound from all around them, depending on how they want to experience their surroundings.
Mark Zuckerberg has made it clear that he believes smart glasses are the future, and it’s evident that his company is doing its best to fulfill that vision. But smart glasses remain a niche that has yet to truly find its footing. What was most obvious at Connect is that Meta has — in an attempt to succeed where others have failed — cast a very wide net, trying to make its glasses stylish, functional, and, most of all, useful.
Is this the future? Unsurprisingly, everyone at Connect seemed to think so. I suppose we’ll have to see if the rest of the world follows suit.

If you download the latest Google Messages update you might not notice anything different at a first glance. However, the brand has introduced several new redesigns that should make the experience more seamless with day-to-day use.
9to5Google shared the changes, giving users a heads-up that it's now even easier to gain access to timestamps in Messages. While you used to have to tap each chat bubble, you can now swipe left across the chat screen to reveal timestamps for all the messages.
It will also show the status, whether it's been delivered or pending, and whether it's secure or not. In order to reply to a message, you will now have to swipe right into the chat bubble. This might take some getting used to, but once you get it down, it should make the overall process much smoother.
In addition, Android Authority shared news about a new long-press command that's now available to experiment with in Messages. While you used to have to tap the menu at the top of a chat to access expanded features, that all changes today.
Going forward, users can long-press a message to open the same menu. The menu will provide quick access to Replay, Forward, Copy, Star, Delete, Select more, and Info. You can also long-press to highlight parts of a message if you want to copy and paste specific text.
Users can now update the app to see whether they have access. Although it's rolling out more widely, it doesn't appear to be available to everyone. For the most part, these two changes are very welcome, providing quality-of-life improvements that we can all enjoy.
Google Messages is still one of the best messaging options. However, that doesn't mean that it can't be improved. We love when Google pushes out changes, and more so when the changes are impactful. Of course, we've discovered that some tweaks need to be done on our own.
