articles.title_zh: 'Stop using threats': China takes veiled shot at US over Cuba & Iran in sharply critical UN speech
articles.content_orig:
Trump likely shrugged off Pezeshkian UN attack as he 'holds the cards,' foreign policy expert says.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital Wednesday.
The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of one another, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount.
"Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu , a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital.
Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression.
THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian holds a picture, which he says is from the Minab school that was hit by an airstrike, as he addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. headquarters Sept. 23, 2026, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
"We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed.
"Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us."
"I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record.
Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faces a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction.
"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday.
While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable.
TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH
President Donald Trump addresses the UNGA in New York City. (Michael Santiago/Getty Images)
"To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said.
"Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now."
Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes.
Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive.
Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports.
KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and President Donald Trump (Majid Saeedi/Getty Images; Jose Luis Magana/AP)
Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other."
But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework.
"It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said.
"In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic."
The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict.
TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian addresses the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters Sept. 23, 2026, in New York City. (Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images)
"Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said.
Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy .
"I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program.
"Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved.

"Of course, the Trump administration is looking for a political win here."

articles.content_orig:
High-stakes discussions on trade and artificial intelligence unfold in New York City as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer meet with Chinese officials. Fox News contributor Dan Hoffman analyzes this strategic framework between the world's two most powerful nations ahead of the upcoming summit with President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
The United States and China agreed to lower tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods traded between the two countries following a three-day summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C.
According to the White House, the $30 billion in reciprocal tariff reductions apply to "non-sensitive goods."
U.S. exports including agricultural products, fish and seafood, logs and wood products, cosmetics and medical devices will receive favorable tariff treatment in China. Meanwhile, U.S. imports of Chinese-made small appliances, toys, holiday decorations and children's car seats will also receive preferential treatment.
The agreement was reached through the U.S.-China Board of Trade, a body first proposed during Trump's visit to China in May and formally established during Xi's visit to Washington this week.
President Donald Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping to speak during a state dinner in the East Room of the White House on Sept. 24, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
XI PRAISES US STATE VISIT 'PERFECTION' AS TRUMP CALLS MEETINGS 'VERY PRODUCTIVE'
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that "a lot more details" about the new trade agreement will be released on Monday.
Greer said the tariff terms were hammered out after weeks of negotiations. Neither country has released the final tariff rates or all the products that will receive favored status going forward.
This marks one of the most significant cooldowns in the trade war Trump launched against China in February 2025, when he levied a 10% tariff on all Chinese imports, citing Beijing's alleged role in the fentanyl crisis and illegal immigration. China hit back with levies on U.S. coal, liquefied natural gas, crude oil and cars.
President Donald Trump holds up a tariff chart while speaking during a "Make America Wealthy Again" trade announcement event in the Rose Garden at the White House on April 2, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
BESSENT REVEALS EXTENSION TO BUSAN AGREEMENT WITH CHINA UNTIL JANUARY
At their peak, U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods reached a staggering 145% in April 2025, shortly after Trump unveiled his "Liberation Day" reciprocal tariffs. China responded with tariffs of up to 125% on U.S. goods.
U.S. and Chinese negotiators met in Geneva in May 2025 and agreed to a 90-day truce that lowered U.S. tariffs to 30% and China's to 10%. The agreement was extended for another 90 days in August.
President Donald Trump walks on a red carpet after greeting Chinese President Xi Jinping during an arrival ceremony on Sept. 23, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Trump and Xi reached another tentative agreement during talks in South Korea in October 2025. Under the deal, China agreed to crack down on fentanyl precursors, resume purchases of U.S. soybeans and ease restrictions on rare-earth exports , while the United States agreed to further ease tariffs.
The two countries will now use the Board of Trade to negotiate additional tariff reductions and other trade disputes, leaving open the possibility of broader agreements in the months ahead.

Amid a fast-growing international debate over regulating artificial intelligence, President Trump and Chinese President Xi met at the White House for several hours on Thursday ahead of a state dinner where several of the biggest players in A.I. were set to attend.
“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. The Administration has offered few updates on the board since then.

articles.title_orig: Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Russell holds off Verstappen in super-close finish, Norris crashes out - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: Azerbaijan Grand Prix: Russell holds off Verstappen in super-close finish, Norris crashes out - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend went the way many believed the 2026 season would play out. George Russell strolled to victory from pole, though with a little late jeopardy, whilst Kimi Antonelli ’s crash in qualifying meant he had to fight his way through the field to finish fifth. That, after all, was the order of things last season.
Yet the past few days in Baku are an inversion of the season’s storyline. It is Antonelli who has been the faster driver, heading for a maiden world title at the second time of asking. Russell has been the troubled one. This was only the Briton’s third victory of the season and his first since Austria in late June. Antonelli has racked up eight wins and, before this weekend in Baku, a well-deserved 81-point lead over Russell.
Russell’s dominant and impressive run from pole to the chequered flag on Saturday is both a reminder of what he is capable of and also what might have been, had he been able to find this type of form earlier and more often. The reality, though, is that he needs to replicate this for the rest of the season to even be in with a sniff, barring a catastrophic meltdown from Antonelli. Still, Russell looked elated to have ended his barren run.
The finish was a little more tense than Russell deserved, having established a healthy lead in the first half of the race. Two late safety cars eradicated his advantage and helped put Max Verstappen’s Red Bull on his gearbox. In the end, he triumphed by just under 0.2sec and, as Antonelli finished fifth – with some help from two safety-car inducing crashes – he made up 15 points on his Mercedes team-mate. Isack Hadjar completed the podium for Red Bull after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.
A drag race to the finish line! 🍿 #F1 #AzerbaijanGP pic.twitter.com/Nb6xfkkpIb
Whether or not this performance is too little from Russell, it is almost certainly too late . The margin to the championship leader is now down to 66 points with a probable seven rounds – including one sprint race – remaining. It improves Russell’s chances of a championship from “unthinkable” to “remote”.
Russell has already written off his own hopes of beating Antonelli to the championship. He did not seem to have changed his mind or his approach after stepping out of his car victoriously.
“Win every race. That’s the game plan,” Russell said. “My team-mate’s had an incredible season, he’s been pretty flawless throughout, but now we’re getting to crunch time.
“I’m just going to focus on myself. If I continue giving performances like I did this weekend, at the end of the season I’ll be happy because it’s been a tough period for me and I’ll feel like I’ve come through the other side.”
In fairness to Russell, his eighth grand prix victory did not come entirely out of nowhere as he has been much closer to Antonelli since the summer break. With a bit more luck in Zandvoort and Monza, he may have been closer still.
“I think it’s just having more experience with this new driving style I’ve adopted and every race since the break I feel like I’ve gone from strength to strength. I feel more like myself again,” he added.
Russell would have had an easier route to victory were it not for the two safety car periods in the second half of the race. The first came out after Alexander Albon slammed his Williams into the barriers at turn five on lap 31 of 51. That bunched the pack up and wiped out the 10-second lead that Russell had built up over Oscar Piastri’s McLaren.
As is so often the case in F1, and especially on street circuits, one safety car often brings about another. And so it was as Franco Colapinto’s enormously optimistic divebomb up the inside of turn one on the lap-36 restart took out not only his Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly, but also McLaren’s Lando Norris.
Absolute chaos at the restart 😵 #F1 #AzerbaijanGP pic.twitter.com/o4Q5MdHLnc
Norris had stern words for Colapinto, who has been handed a five-place grid drop for the next race in Malaysia, after his elimination. “There’s just some drivers that shouldn’t be in Formula One, to be honest,” the reigning world champion said.
“I think the FIA should start handing out bans for this kind of stuff. It’s careless, it costs a lot of money. All my parts are in the bin,” he added.
The greatest pressure Russell faced came after the second restart, after Verstappen moved swiftly into second. The Dutchman, who has yet to win in 2026, is not a driver anybody wants to see fill their mirrors at the best of times, let alone when trying to end a 12-week, six-race win drought.
Yet Verstappen could not find a way past. The most threatening moment of the final 12 laps was on the final push to the chequered flag. articles.title_zh: Tenth woman's body found in South Africa suburb as police probe killings
articles.content_orig:
File photo of South African Police Service officers in Johannesburg
Police in South Africa say that they have found a woman's body in a Johannesburg suburb, the tenth in recent months.
The body was found on Saturday morning and identified by the friend with whom she had been at a bar the previous evening.
The local police commissioner said his force could not rule out the possibility that there was a serial killer on the loose, noting similarities across the 10 deaths in Ekurhuleni, as well as another in Soweto.
The deaths have sparked a national outcry about the scale of violence against women in the country, which has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world.
The latest body was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg.
Police issued a statement a short while later saying crime scene investigators were at the scene gathering evidence. Officials have yet to publicly identify the victim.
The woman's friend told national broadcaster SABC that she recognised her friend's clothes from the previous night when shown a picture of the body.
"I don't know what I'm going to say to her children," she said while wiping away tears. "It's painful."
Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said that, at this early stage in the investigation, it was too soon to say whether the woman's death was linked to the others.
He told reporters that the other bodies shared a "similar victimology" that indicated a shared "modus operandi" of killing, which would allow police to determine whether this latest death was linked to the others.
"For now, it's not something which we can overrule to say there's a serial killer, but we cannot conclusively indicate as such," Lt Gen Mthombeni said.
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates - with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
But it is the nature of the recent killings around Johannesburg that has left many women there reeling from the growing death toll.
The 10 other bodies have been found in similar circumstances to one another since July. Most of them were found in Kempton Park, one neighbourhood over from Tembisa.
Many of the bodies were those of young women and almost all had suffered extreme violence prior to their deaths.
The deaths have placed pressure on the national government less than a year after ministers declared gender-based violence a national disaster.
While South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender, the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed and 1,052 others survived attempted murder between April and June this year.
Three men appeared in court earlier this week accused of being involved in one of the nine murders, with police working to track down others who may have been involved.

The White House has banned CNN reporters from flying with Donald Trump on Air Force One for his upcoming trip to Tennessee , the network says.
Despite a judge’s order restoring CNN’s access to the White House after Trump banned the network , along with MS NOW and Politico, from covering his daily activities, reporters are still being denied entry to certain events.
In the latest roadblock, the White House announced in a Friday night note detailing the president’s schedule that CNN will not be allowed on Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville on Saturday for a college football game, the network reported .
CNN is part of a rotating press pool that covers White House events for major TV networks. No other outlet was listed to replace CNN in the memo, according to the network. Without a designated pooler, major networks won’t be able to televise his trip.
The network’s journalists were also stopped by a press wrangler when they tried to cover Chinese President Xi Jinping’s arrival at the White House for a state dinner Thursday night, the network reported .
The White House reportedly told CNN shortly before the event that it could cover the greeting ceremony but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, despite other networks being allowed to bring reporters and producers.
MS NOW also reported being blocked from the greeting ceremony. “The big question is — is this going to continue? Are we not going to be credentialed into these daily events?” MS NOW White House reporter Laura Barrón-López asked network host Symone Sanders Townsend Thursday night.
But CNN was allowed to cover Trump and Xi’s visit to the National Archives in Washington, D.C., on Friday.
The Independent has reached out to the White House and CNN for comment about the network’s coverage of Trump’s Knoxville trip.
Coverage of the White House has been spotty ever since Trump banned the three networks last Friday, calling them “fake news.”
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” the president wrote on Truth Social.
The outlets then sued to regain access to the White House, arguing the ban violated their First Amendment rights.
In an early morning ruling Thursday, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges.
But reporters were still denied entry later Thursday morning. By Thursday afternoon, reporters regained access to the White House.
The White House TV press pool had abstained from filming in solidarity with the outlets Trump banned until their access was reinstated. CBS served as the designated pooler Friday, filming Xi and Trump at the White House during the final day of his state visit .
Trump’s disdain for the mainstream press is well-documented, including his outbursts at female journalists for asking questions about the Epstein files and the Iran war. He has repeatedly targeted CNN’s Chief White House Correspondent Kaitlan Collins for “not smiling.”
But his attempt to ban several major outlets from the White House is unprecedented.
Former President Bill Clinton — who had an affair with a young staffer, Monica Lewinsky , in the 1990s that dominated the news cycle — said at the Clinton Global Initiative summit earlier this week, “There were lots of times when I wanted to ban the White House press corps.
“And there's a reason we have a Constitution. Because none of us are immune from being pissed off."

Saudi Arabia warned U.N. members Saturday that attempts to block Middle East waterways are a threat to global energy security and demanded the international community do more to defend freedom of navigation.
"The international community has been absent from assuming its responsibilities in confronting all that threatens international peace and security," Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan told the United Nations General Assembly.
"The kingdom stresses the importance of guaranteeing the protection of freedom of navigation in all international waterways, foremost among them the Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden," he said.
The minister further demanded the return of conditions in the Strait of Hormuz to what they were before Feb. 28, without imposing any fees or taxes.
"The kingdom rejects any party's use of these vital passages as a tool for pressure, threat, or harm to the interests of states, in a manner consistent with international law and relevant United Nations resolutions," he said.
Bin Farhan was speaking shortly after President Trump had rejected an Iranian proposal of a deal to reopen Hormuz, in exchange for — among other conditions — a Middle East ceasefire and the release of frozen Iranian assets.
Reopening the Strait of Hormuz has been the focal point of much of the negotiations, but the Saudis have been facing increased difficulties transporting oil due to the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen effectively closing the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern exit to the Red Sea, through targeting Saudi-flagged tankers and attacks on the East-West pipeline through inland Saudi Arabia.
As the world deals with decreasing oil supplies and increasing prices, President Trump asked his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to increase petroleum production in his country, according to the White House.
The White House provided a fact sheet following Mr. Trump's meeting with Xi for a state visit this week that highlights "President Trump urged President Xi to increase production of refined petroleum products to stabilize global supply."
The war with Iran, and its spread to Saudi Arabia, has tightened global energy supplies even as the U.S. has worked to escort tankers out of the Persian Gulf. Mr. Trump said earlier Saturday that 29 vessels had been guided out of the Strait of Hormuz under military supervision.
But the supply of oil and natural gas have still suffered compared to prewar levels. And the revived fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government has now led to the closure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Saudi-flagged oil tankers.
Brent crude, the international standard, closed the week at $104 a barrel, the same as it began the week, despite rising to $108 on Thursday.
Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Russia is ready to help stabilize the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Gulf region, as the U.S.-Iran conflict drags on.
"We need trust in the relationships between the Gulf states, the Arab states and Iran. We need stable regional architecture," Lavrov told leaders Saturday at the U.N. General Assembly.
"Russia, together with other responsible states, stands ready to constructively contribute to stabilizing this strategically important region."
Lavrov did not elaborate on how Russia would provide assistance to end the conflict spreading across the Middle East.
Russia has long been an ally of Iran. Iran provided Shahed drones to Russia for its own invasion of Ukraine. Russia in turn has reportedly assisted Iran with satellite coordination to target U.S. forces in the region.
The Israeli army destroyed an alleged Hezbollah weapons storage facility in southern Lebanon on Saturday.
"Earlier today (Saturday), the IDF struck a weapons storage facility belonging to the Hezbollah terrorist organization in the Sejoud area of southern Lebanon," the IDF said in a statement. "The strike was carried out to remove a threat: the facility stored weapons that were used to target IDF soldiers operating in the Security Zone."
The so-called "security zone" is an area of southern Lebanon set up by Israel that reaches about 6 or 7 miles into the country from the northern Israeli border.
Israel and Hezbollah have signed several short-term ceasefires, mostly recently in late June, but they have all been punctuated by violations from both sides. Deals signed between Israel and the Lebanese government, including the trilateral agreement brokered by the U.S., have each been rejected by Hezbollah.
President Trump has rejected the latest proposal from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days and launch in-depth negotiations to end the war.
"I'm rejecting their deal," Mr. Trump told reporters while leaving the White House on Saturday to travel to Tennessee. "They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they are losing so badly. You don't see that in the fake news. We're winning tremendously, we have total control of the Hormuz Strait, massive amounts of oil are coming out of the Hormuz Strait, last night we had 29 ships come out."
"They want to make a deal," he continued. "I think that's fine, I like making a deal too. But that deal [they offered] would not be acceptable."
Both the U.S. and Iran had expressed optimism over talks held in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, though they were short on details of what was discussed. Mr. Trump did not attend the talks directly, but his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and special envoy Steve Witkoff were involved in the negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.
The deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was reportedly similar to the Islamabad memorandum signed in June, including ending the blockade, allowing Iranian oil sales and halting fighting in every Middle East theater. The U.S. disputed Iran's interpretation of the MOU over who controlled traffic in the strait and the deal fell apart by July.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian had told CBS News' Margaret Brennan on Friday that his country was standing at the ready to implement the new deal.
"If this message reaches the president of the United States, or the interviewers and those involved in the discussions, naturally the process will begin from the very day they accept it," he said.
China pushed back against the United States in its speech at the U.N. General Assembly on Saturday, saying sovereignty of countries in the Gulf should be respected.
Vice President Han Zheng did not mention the U.S. by name in his remarks.
The comments stood in sharp contrast to the friendship on display earlier this week at the White House, where President Trump feted Chinese leader Xi Jinping with military flyovers and at a lavish state dinner.
"Major countries should have special responsibilities for safeguarding international peace and security, and they should take the lead in complying with the rules, upholding rule of law, and doing what's right," Han said.
"China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected," he added.
Trump warned Xi against providing support to Iran during the Washington talks and received assurances that China would not do so, the U.S. ambassador to China said on Friday.
The warning followed reports Beijing had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and Tehran had found ways to evade sanctions on its oil sales with Chinese help.
Iran will not resort to violence in order to counter harsh sanctions against its airline industry imposed by the United States, according to Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, as told to semi-official ISNA news agency.

articles.title_orig: Nor’easter hits Philadelphia region, bringing high waves, coastal flooding to N.J. and Delaware
articles.title_zh: Nor’easter hits Philadelphia region, bringing high waves, coastal flooding to N.J. and Delaware
articles.content_orig:
New York and New Jersey issued a state of emergency as the storm struck.
The early-season nor'easter hit the East Coast Saturday bringing in torrential rain, high winds and flood warnings for millions of people.
Streets in New Jersey and New York, which were under a state of emergency, were already flooded as the storm and high tide combined for dangerous conditions. Waves of 16 feet or more have been reported by buoys off the Jersey Shore and southern New England.
Late Friday night, a weather station in Surf City, New Jersey, reported a wind gust of 74 mph. Other stations along the Jersey Shore have reported wind gusts of 60 mph or more.
The winds toppled trees in New York City, with some landing on top of parked cars.
Tidal flood waters peaked at moderate flood stage late Friday and rose ahead of high tide later Saturday morning.
In Freeport, Long Island, high tide reached major stage, at 7.8 feet, which is the highest in more than two years. High tide In Ocean County, New Jersey, reached 5.7 feet, that's third highest on record.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, who already declared a state of emergency, told reporters Saturday morning that much more rain was coming.
"With tonight's full moon, the tides may even be higher. We expect waves as tall as 20 feet in some areas. Winds will be just as powerful as the waves, wind gusts exceeding 50, even 60 miles an hour, have already been recorded on Long Island," she said at a news conference.
The governor added that power outages were expected throughout the state and warned residents to be prepared.
Subways and trains have been operating as expected so far, according to the governor. Storm doors have been added at rail yards at Coney Island and Howard Beach to reduce the chance of impacts on service, Hochul said.
"Here's the bottom line: Stay out of the water. Although we just saw a surfer on one of the cameras off the coast of Long Island, stay out of the water," she said. "Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life."
Suffolk County Executive Ed Romaine told reporters that 17,000 residents have lost power in the Long Island county and he expects more outages over the next 24 hours.
"Montauk is getting hit with 50 mile an hour winds. Our concern is that trees will topple, and with them, power lines," he said.
Parts of the southern Chesapeake Bay to the Jersey Shore and into the Raritan Bay reached moderate to major flood stage from coastal flooding during high tide Saturday morning. While the tide has begun to recede, some of these areas mentioned are still dealing with moderate to major coastal flooding.
Coastal flood alerts remain in effect from eastern Virginia through southern Maine, including Virginia Beach, Philadelphia, New York City, New London, Connecticut, Providence, Rhode Island, and Boston.
Moderate to major coastal flooding is possible during high tide later Saturday evening from the southern Chesapeake Bay to the Jersey Shore and up to Raritan Bay.
Wind advisories remain in effect from the Delmarva Peninsula up to eastern Massachusetts, including Dover, Delaware; Philadelphia; New York City; Hartford, Connecticut; and Worcester, Massachusetts, for winds gusting up to 45 mph.
High wind warnings are in effect for the Jersey Shore, as well as parts of Rhode Island and Massachusetts, including Boston, Providence and Atlantic City, for winds gusting up to 60 mph. The winds can knock down trees and power lines.
High waves of 6 to 12 feet or more will continue to pound the coastline from coastal Delmarva through the Jersey Shore, Long Island and southeastern coastal New England, producing widespread and potentially significant beach erosion and dangerous coastal conditions.
Per police in Stafford Township, New Jersey, the Route 72 causeway into Long Beach Island has been closed to non-essential personnel.
According to the National Weather Service, evacuations were underway for hotels in the vicinity along Black Horse Pike in New Jersey earlier this morning. Parts of the Black Horse Pike are underwater in multiple places, resulting in the closure of the roadway.
On Saturday afternoon and evening, rounds of heavy rain and strong wind gusts will continue from Maryland to southern New York and begin stretching into southern New England. High tide around 9 p.m. could produce moderate coastal flooding, with some isolated major coastal flooding possible.
Overnight into Sunday morning, rounds of heavy rain and strong wind gusts will continue from Maryland to southern New England as several rounds of heavy rain will move through before sunrise, with isolated instances of inland flash flooding possible.
The nor’easter will continue to linger on Sunday but begin to break up and weaken. Winds and rain will begin to lighten, though gusty winds and some heavier pockets of rain will remain possible with potential lingering impacts into Monday.
Rainfall totals will be widespread at 2 to 4 inches across the Northeast, with some of the highest totals reaching up to 6 inches from New Jersey to Boston.
Some inland flash flooding will be possible, especially in areas with poor drainage, where blown leaves can clog storm drains, or where the heaviest bands of rain move through.
However, because the rain is falling over such a long duration, inland flash flooding will not be the most widespread threat as wind-driven rain could instead lead to power outages.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in Paris
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo celebrates open-air mass before 700,000 people in Paris
articles.content_orig:
Crowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 years
Hundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in ⁠Paris on Saturday to attend an open-air mass with Pope Leo, on the second day of his visit to France .
The Vatican estimated 700,000 people turned out for the outdoor mass with the 71-year-old American pope – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend.
It took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic.
The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life.
But cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked ‌God in his homily for the chance to ‌visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promote Catholicism and its teachings.
It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.
Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.”
He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness.
“Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said.
The security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.
Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances.
He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.
About 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops.
Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.”
Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”

articles.title_orig: Trump says he has rejected Iranian proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.title_zh: Trump says he has rejected Iranian proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, after Iranian officials indicated that shipping through the critical waterway could resume within days if a deal was sealed.
“I rejected their deal. They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump told reporters as he boarded Marine One on the White House lawn, after indirect talks between the two countries were held on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York.
“What they wanted is to immediately open the Hormuz Strait. You know why? Because they’re dying. You know why they’re dying? Because they have no money coming in because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait,” he continued. “They outsmarted themselves. They said, ‘Let’s close it and cause a problem for the world.’ And I came along, and we put up the greatest blockade ever in military history.”
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected Iran’s offer to revive a ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz .
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said Friday that the choice “rests with the United States.”
“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi told reporters.
He said a “concrete seven-day plan” that includes reopening the strait had been conveyed to the U.S. through mediator Qatar and was ready to start “as soon as the United States accepts this plan.”
Iran offers new proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Araghchi said the actions required of the U.S. in Iran’s proposal were commitments already agreed to in the June memorandum of understanding between the two countries that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. That agreement, signed in June, collapsed within days after fresh strikes were exchanged.
One of the conditions of the plan is for the U.S. to accept a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz that has been agreed upon by Iran and Oman , Araghchi had said Thursday.
A U.S. official said on Friday that the Trump administration was having positive and constructive discussions through the mediators but that it was not in any hurry to reach an agreement.
“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush,” the U.S. official said. “Over the last 48 hours, nearly 40 million barrels of oil have transited the strait.”
Earlier this week, Trump said he was still considering whether to “annihilate” Iran or make a deal. Early Saturday, he posted an image to Truth Social of the Strait of Hormuz labeled the “Trump Strait.”
In an interview with Al Jazeera on Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that resolving the Hormuz issue “is possible through negotiations, not the use of force,” but warned that his country does not “trust” talks with Washington.
Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.
Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.
“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations, two days after Trump said he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after the elections .
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”
Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November midterms. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while 69% disapproved.
The U.S. this week announced it would impose sanctions on any global companies doing business ​with Iranian airlines, with the aim of grounding Iran’s entire civil fleet worldwide.
Iraq said Saturday that it was engaging with the U.S. in an effort to restore humanitarian flights to and from Iran, after Iranian airlines were barred from neighboring countries in response to the sanctions.
Efforts were ongoing to “secure exemptions for certain Iraqi airports from these measures” in order to enable “the resumption of flights for humanitarian reasons, such as medical treatment, education, religious pilgrimages, and the interests of civilians,” the Iraqi prime minister’s office said.
Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that flights had also been shut down to Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan.
Freddie Clayton is a freelance journalist based in London.

articles.title_orig: Nolo still meandering south of Hawaiʻi Island as a Category 2 hurricane
articles.title_zh: Nolo still meandering south of Hawaiʻi Island as a Category 2 hurricane
articles.content_orig:
By CHRIS MELORE, US DEPUTY SCIENCE EDITOR
Published: 10:00 EDT, 26 September 2026 | Updated: 11:00 EDT, 26 September 2026
Hurricane Nolo is expected to cause 'catastrophic flooding' as the life-threatening storm nears the Hawaiian islands and over one million Americans this weekend.
A state of emergency has already been issued in Hawaii and forecasters now believe the strengthening hurricane could bring historic levels of rainfall, particularly across the Big Island (also known as Hawaii Island).
AccuWeather forecasters warned that the week-long deluge could dump as much as 55 inches of rain on the Big Island - just under five feet of precipitation.
If that prediction is correct, Nolo would be the second wettest hurricane in Hawaii's history, falling just behind Hurricane Lane's 58 inches in 2018.
The National Hurricane Center (NHC) said in a statement: 'Life-threatening, catastrophic flooding and mudslides are possible, especially in areas of steep terrain across the eastern and southern portions of the Big Island and Maui.'
Local officials on the islands have also urged residents and tourists to be prepared to evacuate flood-prone areas as the hurricane makes its closest approach.
Although Nolo is not projected to make landfall, AccuWeather has projected that at least two to four inches of rain will fall across the entire island chain. The hurricane is currently about 140 miles from Hawaii.
Both Maui and the Big Island are also expected to be struck by dangerous and sustained wind gusts reaching between 60 and 80 mph through Monday.
Hurricane Nolo is expected to become a Category 4 hurricane this weekend with winds over 130 mph
Residents in Hawaii began preparing for potentially catastrophic flooding this week
Nolo erupted into a tropical storm on Wednesday less than 400 miles south of the Hawaiian islands and has been slowly gaining strength throughout the week.
AccuWeather and NHC have both warned that Nolo will likely reach major hurricane status by Saturday afternoon, growing into a Category 3 storm with sustained winds exceeding 111 mph.
Saturday is expected to be the peak of the threat for Hawaii, as the hurricane makes its closest approach to land.
The worst of the rain and possible hurricane-force winds are expected to hit the exposed slopes of the Big Island's eastern side. Forecasts have predicted that this side of the island will see at least two feet of rain.
Maui, a major tourist destination just 30 miles to the west of the Big Island, will also see increasing rain and possible tropical storm conditions on Saturday, as winds range between 40 and 60 mph.
Mayor Richard Bissen of Maui County said in a statement : 'During this above-normal hurricane season, recent storms remind us that we cannot afford to be complacent.'
'Our top priority is the safety of our community. Now is the time for all of us to review household emergency plans, check supplies and make sure you can receive important alerts and information.'
National Weather Service officials in Honolulu warned: 'Leave immediately if evacuation orders are given for your area.'
Hurricane Lala caused at least two deaths and billions of dollars in damage from flooding and mudslides in August
Forecasters have warned that more than three feet of rain could fall on Hawaii's Big Island
A prediction of 55 inches of rain by AccuWeather would make Hurricane Nolo the second wettest hurricane in Hawaii's history
Hawaii's Big Island is home to more than 200,000 people, and the island is still recovering from the devastating effects of Hurricanes Lala and Lowell this summer.
The storm destroyed over 100 homes, damaged hundreds more and killed at least five people across the state, with the heaviest damage occurring on the Big Island during Lala's approach on August 15.
Downpours, flooding and mudslides, similar to what is expected during Nolo, led to more than 100 homes on the Big Island being washed away during the August hurricane.
Hurricane Lowell struck the opposite end of the island chain in September, causing widespread power outages and property damage on the islands of Kauaʻi and Niʻihau.
Emergency shelters have been opened on the Big Island ahead of the hurricane's arrival.
Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda said in a statement: 'If your home flooded before, or is at risk, consider moving to safer shelter before the full force of the storm hits. Because the ground remains saturated, flooding may happen rapidly.'
By Sunday, Nolo is expected to start moving away from Hawaii, although the hurricane will likely continue strengthening, growing into a Category 4 storm with winds surpassing 130 mph.
Rain and flooding will likely continue before gradually easing heading into the new week.

Investors looking to boost their exposure to artificial intelligence should target China, according to Matthews Asia portfolio manager Andrew Mattock.
He said investors will need a more deliberate approach because broad emerging market strategies won't be that effective.
"Investors need to be aware when they buy an emerging market fund or when they buy a plain vanilla MSCI product… they're not getting a lot of it," Mattock told CNBC's "ETF Edge" this week. "The big piece that you are missing… is the Chinese piece."
He noted that companies from South Korea and Taiwan comprise almost half of the iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF (EEM) while the iShares MSCI China ETF (MCHI) lacks a focus on AI stocks.
Mattock is behind the Matthews China Fund (MCHFX) . The fund invests at least 80% of its net assets in  the common and preferred stocks of companies located in China, according to the firm's website.
The fund is off 4% so far this year, as of Friday's close. Its largest holdings include Tencent and Alibaba .
It appears investing in China is seeing a meaningful shift.
Billionaire hedge fund manager David Tepper, founder of Appaloosa Management, found the world's second economy attractive again – telling CNBC in September 2024 that he bought more of "everything" related to China.
However, KraneShares' Brendan Ahern recommended that investors consider strategies that could protect them from wild market swings in China.
"I like the idea of utilizing options around some of those ETFs…  like with KWEB [KraneShares CSI China Internet ETF]," the firm's chief investment officer said in the same interview.
"Why do some of these hedge funds gravitate to these ETFs? Because they're able to write a call and principally protect themselves," he added. "Give themselves some downside."
According to FactSet, the KraneShares CSI China Internet ETF has the same top two holdings as the Matthews China Fund: Tencent and Alibaba. But as of Friday's close, the fund is down more than 27% so far this year.

articles.title_orig: Body of 10th woman found in South Africa as killings investigation continues
articles.title_zh: Body of 10th woman found in South Africa as killings investigation continues
articles.content_orig:
South African police said Saturday that another woman's body had been found near Johannesburg, bringing the number of victims to 10 in a series of killings under investigation.
Police began investigating after the bodies of three women were found in July and August within about 4.3 miles of one another in the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.
The discovery of six bodies in Ekurhuleni over 10 days earlier this month raised fears that a serial killer or killers were responsible.
Two women were arrested and charged last week with murder in relation to the ninth body , discovered on Sept. 17. The victim had been stabbed and had her throat cut, police said. Police did not link the two women charged to any of the other killings.
Provincial police commissioner Lt. Gen. Tommy Mthombeni told state broadcaster SABC on Saturday that investigators believed the ninth killing was an isolated case but could not rule out the possibility that some of the other cases were linked.
Police had issued a warning for women to use caution while in the area.
Police have identified similarities in some of the killings but said they had not found conclusive evidence that the same person or people were responsible.
All nine of the bodies discovered before Saturday were those of women in their 20s or 30s, according to police. Several were naked or partially clothed and left in open areas near main roads. Officers from the Investigative Psychology Unit, which specializes in complex or serial violent crimes, are part of the investigation.
Police released limited details about the 10th body, which was found early Saturday, and did not immediately identify the victim.
"We can only confirm the discovery of the body," the South African Police Service said in a statement. "Crime scene management and all the necessary role players are currently on the scene."
South Africa has high rates of violent crime and violence against women. Three women were killed every day by an intimate partner from 2020-2021, a recent study found.
The country has one of the highest global murder rates , with more than 60 a day on average.
The killings in Ekurhuleni have sparked a national outcry over women's safety.

articles.title_orig: For the Indiana Fever, the playoff spotlight has never been brighter as they match up with reigning champion Aces: 'Everybody's watching'
articles.title_zh: For the Indiana Fever, the playoff spotlight has never been brighter as they match up with reigning champion Aces: 'Everybody's watching'
articles.content_orig:
The text messages began flooding Makayla Timpson 's phone in August. Names of people she hadn't spoken to in years. New numbers she didn't recognize.
People who knew her even tangentially wanted to congratulate the second-year forward on moving into the starting lineup, where she stayed for the final 13 games of the regular season.
It's hard to miss such news when the Fever are inescapable.
"Everybody's watching," Timpson told Yahoo Sports the day of an Aug. 18 victory in Toronto . "All of our games are everywhere. We're the team with the games broadcasted all over the place."
The Fever concluded their 44-game regular season — the only team to play every game on national television — with a whimper. Their 86-66 loss to No. 1 seed Minnesota , combined with results elsewhere on the final day of the regular season, pushed them down into the No. 6 seed for the third consecutive season despite realistic expectations they would nab a top-four seed.
There are thoughts about that. Fans fire off takes on social media platforms in short and long form. Surely, there is chatter over meals in Indiana and everywhere else, given the team is regularly watched by more than 1 million people per game, a metric previously unthinkable. This is a defining characteristic of their entire 2026 season that included unrelenting speculation surrounding superstar Caitlin Clark and head coach Stephanie White verbally ripping an "online community" of divisiveness attempting to "hijack our league," among other topics.
For the Fever, it's all white noise. They have focused on blocking out everything — or nearly everything — that does not reside within their walls. The franchise's awards season marketing campaign leaned into the idea, sending out boomboxes and cassette tapes for each of its candidates. The jackets listed records and elite stats. The tapes played loud, coupled with tape hiss, a broadcast call of their highlights.
Everything featured the running tagline "We don't do quiet."
The postseason will give them the true answer. Will it be an early exit, or a loud stomp that they can live up to championship intentions amid the rising fervor that comes with such a stage? Because this Fever team, despite underperforming in the standings, remains a dangerous championship contender facing the ultimate final test.
"At this point, everybody's record is 0-0," Clark said after the finale. "We're going into the playoffs."
Their supercharged backcourt of MVP candidates Clark and Kelsey Mitchell lived up to the bill. Mitchell (24.7 ppg) — coming off a concerning Rhabdomyolysis condition in Game 5 of the 2025 semifinals — and Clark (22.3 ppg) — returning to form after missing all but 13 games of last season with soft tissue injuries — are second and third in average scoring.
Not on their team — in the entire league.
They lead the Fever's record-shattering offense (96 ppg), made up of a formerly mind-boggling 20 games scoring at least 100 points. The previous record was 11. Their 4,222 total points are nearly 200 more than the second-place Las Vegas Aces (4,025).
In the dark of the flashy numbers, the Fever underperformed, even considering the competition among the eight playoff teams is tight. Only one series matchup, the No. 1 Lynx versus No. 8 Liberty, had been decided by Thursday night. It took the final 64 seconds of the season for the Golden State Valkyries to finish off a 16-point comeback over the Los Angeles Sparks , securing the No. 2 seed and ultimately sending Sparks second-year leader Lynne Roberts packing .
They'll now have an uphill climb through the playoffs, first facing an experienced Las Vegas team beginning on the reigning champions' home court (Sunday, 4 p.m. ET). The Aces are on a run of three WNBA titles in four years, edging the injury-riddled "Hospital Fever" roster in a deciding semifinals Game 5 in Las Vegas last season. None of Clark, Mitchell or center Aliyah Boston , who missed the second half of the Lynx game due to a lower leg injury flare-up, were on the court for overtime. Aces center A'ja Wilson (26.2 ppg, league lead) is in line for a fifth MVP this October , and along with Jackie Young motor the WNBA's second-best offense (91.5 ppg).
The travel doesn't make it any less challenging for Indiana, which had a chance at the No. 4 seed and rights to host the first game of the series. Game 2 is on Wednesday in Indianapolis, and an if-necessary Game 3 back in Las Vegas on Friday. Indiana won the season series, 2-1, with the loss coming on a buzzer-beating bucket in overtime.
On Indiana's side of the bracket is No. 2 Golden State, a matchup that would put to bed (at least for this season) the philosophical argument that defense wins championships. While the Fever lead the league offensively, the Valkyries were far and away the WNBA's best defense throughout the year. They hold teams to under 75.1 points per game on average. The Fever scored 75, 88 and 90 against them, winning only the highest-scoring affair.
White said following the season finale loss that the Fever don't shoot as they did very often, a message of upside, that they got it out of their system. Despite good early looks that would usually spell big leads, few went down for Indiana on Thursday. It was their lowest field-goal percentage (34.3%) and scoring total (66 points) of the season, though the bench rode out the final quarter. They've scored fewer than 80 only five times. Four are losses.
"It's 0-0, and we're still playing basketball," White, who led the Fever to the Finals in 2015 before returning in 2025, said. "And so we flush this one, we learn from it, we grow from it, and we start our prep [for Vegas]."
The offense will need to carry them, studded by glimpses of elite defense at the right moments. It's that side of the ball that has let them down, and could spell their demise. They allow opponents on average 90.4 points per game, fifth-worst in the league and four places away from the Liberty (86.4), the next-closest playoff team. (The Aces took a step back on that side of the ball this year, entering the postseason sixth overall, allowing 85.8 ppg).
Rarely do teams lacking in defense lift the trophy. Nor do seeds outside the top four. Only in 2021 did a team seeded fifth or sixth reach the Finals, when the No. 6 Sky defeated the No. 5 Mercury, 3-1, in the former best-of-five format. Now a best-of-seven, the Fever have nine wins ahead of them to win the franchise's first championship since 2012 and only the second overall.
A championship window, such as the one in which the Fever reside, is always ready to close. It takes a future-focused front office to hold it open. The 2027 books will need a creative mathematician to keep it all together.
Mitchell, the franchise's longest-tenured player on a supermax $1.4 million deal, is an unrestricted free agent. Boston's EPIC deal provision will kick in at $1.47M. Clark, set to still make a rookie-deal $597,596, will be in line to sign one, including a higher salary next year. Sixth Player candidate Sophie Cunningham , point guard back-up Tyasha Harris , who sustained an ankle injury and had to be carried off on Thursday, and Myisha Hines-Allen , who moved to the bench, are all UFAs. The salary cap will increase a currently undetermined amount in the first offseason under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA) based on revenue-sharing.
Then there are players like Timpson, the Fever's second-round pick in the 2025 draft. She averaged 2.6 points in 7.1 minutes per game as a rookie, showing glimpses of upside but not enough consistency on a roster riddled with injuries. After the team overperformed to within minutes of a Finals appearance, the coaching staff traveled to Unrivaled in the offseason to challenge her; she returned to town early to hone in on the task at hand. She's averaging 9 points, 6.3 rebounds, 0.8 blocks and shooting 60% as a starter.

articles.title_orig: White House blocks CNN from traveling with Trump on Air Force One
articles.title_zh: White House blocks CNN from traveling with Trump on Air Force One
articles.content_orig:
The White House is barring CNN from flying on Air Force One on Saturday as part of the news outlet’s duties covering the president on behalf of major television networks.
CNN had been scheduled to fly aboard the president’s plane on his trip to Tennessee for a college football game as part of the White House TV press pool — a small, rotating group of journalists that cover the president in areas where space is limited and share the information they gather with other TV networks.
The move — announced Friday night in a White House note that lays out the president’s schedule — represents the Trump administration’s latest salvo against CNN and the broader White House press corps. No outlet was listed as replacing CNN, meaning there will be no television pool coverage of his trip.
Last week, President Donald Trump announced he was banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. The move also prevented CNN from flying on Air Force One and fulfilling its scheduled pool duties when Trump traveled to the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
A judge later blocked the administration from enforcing the White House ban on the three outlets and ordered it to restore the credentials of the affected reporters. The status of the White House pool, though, was murkier.
With CNN banned, the other TV outlets — Fox, NBC, ABC and CBS — refused to perform their duties until regular access was restored. But regular coverage resumed on Friday, with CNN serving as part of the pool as Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited the National Archives.
It was unclear how the White House’s move might affect CNN, MS NOW and Politico’s litigation. The outside lawyer representing CNN had previously told anchor Jake Tapper he believed the restoration of the outlets’ access included the White House pool. MS NOW and Politico are a part of separate pool rotations from the five major TV networks.
A judge has given the news organizations until Monday to file a request for a preliminary injunction — which would put Trump’s promised ban on hold for a longer period of time.
A CNN spokesperson declined to comment. CNN has reached out to the White House for comment.
In two posts on Truth Social Saturday morning, Trump said CNN and MS NOW should not be allowed in the White House, calling the organizations “perpetrators of FAKE NEWS.”
Later that morning, as he took questions from reporters while departing for Knoxville, an MS NOW reporter asked Trump if he only wants outlets that support him to be part of the White House press pool, to which Trump responded, “I want real news, not fake news.”
“I love an open, free press. What I don’t like is the fake press,” Trump said as he singled out MS NOW and CNN. “What we don’t want is — we don’t want fake news.”
The Washington Post was first to report the White House’s decision.
The TV pool is the primary way that people around the world watch Trump’s speeches and appearances because it supplies video feeds and information to other news organizations.
“That’s the system that allows the networks to share video of the president with the whole country. If they aren’t there, the pool can’t function,” the current president of the White House Correspondents’ Association, Jacqui Heinrich, said on “Fox News Sunday.”
“And America cannot have state TV,” her guest Weijia Jiang of CBS, who was Heinrich’s predecessor as WHCA president, said.
“That’s what makes America America,” she said. “That’s why we need independent coverage, and that’s why this press pool system has been set up for so long and why it works – because you need independent actors to be able to be the observers.”
Along with the TV pool, there are also print, radio and still photography pools. This system exists partly because presidents travel and speak in places where the wider press corps cannot be present.
The Trump White House also produces its own content, including live streams of events.
But, as Jiang put it, “if the government is only showing you what it wants, then you have to question, what are we missing? And that’s what the pool, that’s what these outlets bring to the table.”
This story has been updated with additional details.
CNN’s Logan Schiciano contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: White House Removes CNN From Planned Weekend Trip
articles.title_zh: White House Removes CNN From Planned Weekend Trip
articles.content_orig:
The White House on Friday night removed CNN from joining President Donald Trump on his trip to Tennessee on Saturday, where it was supposed to cover the president on behalf of major TV networks.
According to media guidance sent out by the White House on Friday night, CNN was removed from the list of outlets designated for pool coverage of Trump’s trip, in which he is set to attend a college football game in Knoxville.
The pool is a rotating group of networks that share duties of filming the president both in Washington and on official trips. Other member networks — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — briefly boycotted participating in the pool this week after Trump banned CNN from serving as a member.
CNN on Friday reported that it had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One on Saturday as part of its pool duties covering the president’s trip to the game between the University of Texas and the University of Tennessee. However in the president’s schedule released Friday night, CNN was not listed as a member of the pool and no other network was listed as replacing it.
The move is the latest development in the White House’s attempt to restrict access by CNN and other outlets to cover the White House. The president last week had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House before a judge temporarily blocked that move Thursday and ordered the administration to restore their reporters’ credentials for 14 days.
But while the order restored the outlets’ access to the White House, it didn’t explicitly require the administration to restore CNN’s participation in the television pool.
The White House did not immediately return a request for comment.
Casey Wooten is a breaking news editor for the politics team at NBC News.

President Donald Trump lashed out over his press coverage again Saturday morning after a federal judge ordered him to immediately lift a White House ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW.
In two early morning Truth Social posts, Trump questioned why journalists should have access to the “very sacred” White House. The posts came shortly after his administration barred CNN from Air Force One Saturday and replaced the outlet with LindellTV for his trip to Knoxville, Tennessee, to attend a college football game.
“Why should perpetrators of FAKE NEWS, like CNN and MSDNC, be allowed access to a very sacred place, the White House?” Trump demanded. “Despite my big Election Win, almost 100% of ‘TRUMP’ coverage is negative, and has been for years!”
Less than two hours later, Trump escalated his criticism.
“FAKE NEWS SHOULD NOT BE ALLOWED IN THE WHITE HOUSE!!! IT HAS GONE ON FAR TOO LONG, AT A TREMENDOUS COST TO OUR COUNTRY,” he wrote.
The latest clash with the media began September 18, when Trump abruptly announced that CNN, MS NOW and Politico would be barred from the White House . According to reports, the ban came hours after his aide Natalie Harp showed him videos of unflattering news coverage.
“Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”
By the following morning, CNN, MS NOW and Politico all said that their journalists had been stopped from accessing the White House grounds, with some reporters saying that they were asked to hand over their badges.
On September 21, the outlets filed a lawsuit against Trump and several of his top aides, arguing that the ban violates the Fifth Amendment’s Due Process Clause, as well as the First Amendment, and calls for the press passes to be restored.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the lawsuit states.
The Justice Department has argued that Trump has the authority to ban the outlets on “ national security ” grounds, claiming that “access to the White House is a privilege—not a right.”
On September 24, U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the Trump administration to temporarily reinstate the outlets’ press badges. By that afternoon, reporters regained access to the White House .
Yet, on September 25, the White House announced that CNN will not be allowed on Air Force One when Trump flies to Knoxville, Tennessee, on Saturday for a college football game, the network reported .
CNN is part of a rotating press pool that covers White House events for major TV networks.
Instead, the White House listed LindellTV, a conservative online video platform founded by Trump ally Mike Lindell , on the Air Force One Saturday schedule. Real America’s Voice was also listed.
“I love an open free press,” Trump told reporters Saturday morning before departing from the White House on Marine One.
“What I don’t like is fake news, and they’re fake news 100 percent,” he said, referring to the three outlets he banned. “In two years I doubt they did one good story.”
Trump has long had an extremely combative relationship with the press , accusing reporters of unfair and biased coverage, lobbing personal insults against them and insinuating that those he opposes should be punished.
The president previously curtailed The Associated Press from accessing certain presidential spaces in 2025 after the outlet continued using the “Gulf of Mexico” despite Trump rebranding it as the “Gulf of America.” In 2018, Trump also revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s press pass following a contentious news conference.
