articles.title_orig: Is Ethiopia on the verge of another civil war as fighting erupts in Tigray?
articles.title_zh: Is Ethiopia on the verge of another civil war as fighting erupts in Tigray?
articles.content_orig:
Intensified fighting between Ethiopia’s federal army and forces from the northern region of Tigray has raised fears that the peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war in 2022 could collapse.
The escalation came days after seven armed groups from across Ethiopia formed a new alliance which seeks to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, with each side of the conflict blaming the other for instigating the latest flare-up in violence.
The immediate fear for many in the country is a return to the war they have spent nearly four years trying to recover from. Here is what we know.
The Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, began as an armed movement against Ethiopia’s military government in the 1970s. It later became the dominant force in the coalition that governed Ethiopia for nearly three decades.
That influence was contentious in a country with many ethnic groups, where Tigrayans account for only about 6 percent of Ethiopia’s population. When Abiy became prime minister in 2018, he created the Prosperity Party to replace the governing coalition, sharply reducing the TPLF’s influence at the centre of government.
Relations between Abiy’s government and the TPLF deteriorated until war broke out in November 2020. Federal troops, Eritrean forces and some fighters from the neighbouring Amhara region fought against Tigrayan forces. The conflict killed hundreds of thousands of people, displaced millions and left Tigray largely cut off from the outside world.
A peace agreement signed in Pretoria, South Africa, in November 2022 ended the full-scale war. But it did not settle some of the disputes that had helped fuel it.
One of the deepest disputes concerns western Tigray. Fighters from the neighbouring Amhara region, who fought alongside Ethiopia’s federal army during the 2020-2022 war, took control of western Tigray. Hundreds of thousands of Tigrayans were driven from their homes, and Tigrayan leaders now want the territory returned and those displaced to be allowed to return to their homes.
Many in Amhara reject Tigray’s claim to the territory, however. They argue that western Tigray should not have been incorporated into Tigray when Ethiopia’s regional boundaries were redrawn in 1992, after the fall of the military government.
That dispute is ongoing, even though the TPLF and the Amhara Fano National Movement have now joined the same alliance against Abiy Ahmed’s government.
The federal government also says Tigrayan forces have retained weapons they were meant to surrender. Tigrayan leaders, in turn, say the government has failed to secure the withdrawal of other forces or enable displaced people to return home, particularly to western Tigray.
The political arrangements made after the war have also broken down. The TPLF faction led by Debretsion Gebremichael retook control of Tigray’s administration earlier this year, displacing an interim administration established under the peace agreement.
“Since the end of the war, while the Pretoria Agreement has held, there have been consistent violations on both sides,” Jervin Naidoo, a senior political analyst at Oxford Economics Africa, told Al Jazeera. He said Tigrayans remained aggrieved over western Tigray, the presence of outside forces and the region’s autonomy.
The government sees the TPLF differently. Naidoo said it would portray the group as “a belligerent group trying to destabilise Ethiopia”. But for Tigrayan leaders, he said, renewed fighting could be presented as a matter of protecting their region.
The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival was announced this month by seven armed movements. Its largest members include the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA). It also includes groups from Ethiopia’s Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz areas.
They have different aims and histories, but share a stated objective – to remove Abiy’s government.
Their agreement marks a striking reversal of the alliances formed during the last war, with Fano fighters who fought alongside federal troops against the TPLF now fighting alongside the TPLF.
The Pretoria agreement helped reshape those relationships. It ended the war between Addis Ababa and the TPLF, but Eritrea and Amhara forces, which had supported the government, were not parties to it. Both later fell out with Abiy’s government.
The alliance extends beyond northern Ethiopia. The OLA has fought federal forces in Oromia, in central Ethiopia, since 2018, while a faction of the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) has joined despite a separate peace agreement signed with the government that year. The ONLF leadership inside Ethiopia’s Somali region says it is not part of the new coalition.
Common opposition to Abiy does not mean the groups agree on Ethiopia’s future. Tigrayan and Amhara members still have competing claims to western Tigray. The government has also accused Eritrea of backing the alliance. Eritrea has repeatedly denied supporting the armed groups.
Small-scale clashes and reported drone strikes preceded this week’s escalation. Fighting then intensified in southern Tigray and spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions.
Each side blames the other for starting the latest major clashes. Tigrayan forces say they responded to a federal offensive involving ground troops and drones. The government side accuses the TPLF of attacking first. With the fighting continuing, claims about individual attacks and territorial gains are difficult to verify independently.
“There has been overnight fighting in the border town of Abala,” Al Jazeera’s Catherine Soi reported from Kenya. The town, located in northern Afar on the border with Tigray, was also affected by the previous war. Reports have differed over who controls the town. On a separate front in Amhara, Ethiopia’s army says it killed more than 270 rebel fighters. That figure has not been independently verified.
Tigrayan forces have taken control of the airports at Mekelle, Axum and Shire, disrupting civilian flights. The African Union says the seizure is inconsistent with the Pretoria agreement. About three-quarters of a million people remained displaced within Tigray because of the earlier war before this latest escalation.
There is a risk it could, but analysts say the conflict has not descended into a full-scale civil war yet. Fighting has crossed Tigray’s borders, and the federal government is already facing armed conflicts in other regions.
There is also a chance of regional escalation. Eritrea fought alongside the Ethiopian government during the previous Tigray war, but relations between the neighbours have since deteriorated, partly over Abiy’s push for access to Red Sea ports. Addis Ababa accuses Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia.
The African Union has called for an immediate halt to the escalation and for renewed talks under the Pretoria agreement. It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who helped mediate the 2022 deal, to engage the parties urgently. The East African bloc IGAD has also urged neighbouring countries to avoid actions that could make the crisis worse.

articles.title_orig: Third suspect arrested in death of Mississippi woman found hanging at ‘staged’ crime scene
articles.title_zh: Third suspect arrested in death of Mississippi woman found hanging at ‘staged’ crime scene
articles.content_orig:
A third person has been arrested in the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old woman who police said was found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned Mississippi home in August.
Eric Clark, 45, surrendered to police on Friday and is charged with murder. Police also disclosed on Friday that according to an autopsy investigation, “the scene and the hanging were staged.”
No other details were released about the scene or Fortune’s killing.
Clark is expected to appear in court on Monday.
Two other people, Earnest Lloyd Jr. and Jarques Ratliff , were also arrested and charged with murder in connection with her death. Both men are Black.
Police have released very little information about what led up to Fortune’s death. Detectives investigating the case have interviewed as many as 15 people, collected forensic evidence and followed numerous leads, police said in a news release.
Authorities said Ratliff, 51, had an “association” with Fortune but did not release further details.
Lloyd, 25, allegedly had a physical altercation with Fortune either days or minutes before she died, according to NBC affiliate WLBT of Jackson . Police accused Lloyd of hanging Fortune with a black cable cord, WLBT reported.
Ratliff, who pleaded not guilty , and Lloyd were denied bond at separate court hearings.
Minyvonne Burke is a senior breaking news reporter for NBC News.

The Election Commission of India (ECI) on Saturday (September 26, 2026) announced a slew of measures addressing concerns over the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls across the country, including stopping physical hearings for unmapped voters or those with logical discrepancies in their enumeration forms.
It said that the declaration accompanying Form 6 (used for fresh voter registration) is mandatory only during the current SIR process. This in effect means that new voters who seek inclusion in electoral rolls after the ongoing SIR need not submit any such declaration.
The commission also said that any person whose name has got left out during SIR or thereafter, and any person including young/ first-time voters, may apply to the electoral registration officer (ERO) concerned, for inclusion of their names in the electoral rolls.  A special drive will immediately be launched for their enrolment, it said in a press note.
The SIR process has already been completed in 20 States and Union Territories.
The fresh initiatives of the poll body came after a meeting of the full bench of the commission on Saturday afternoon (September 26, 2026) and days after reports emerged of a rift within the Election Commissioners over these and other issues in the SIR process as well as the internal working of the ECI.
The press note confirmed that the two Commissioners had written to the Cabinet Secretary but said it was not related to any policy matter of the commission or IT division but related to working of an officer on deputation to the ECI. “The work re-distribution orders issued by the concerned officer were not actually implemented after the orders of the two Commissioners,” it clarified.
The commission’s press note was pertinently accompanied by a photograph of all the three Election Commissioners and mentioned that it “has the approval of the full commission”.
As far as physical hearings were concerned, the statement said: “In case of any person to whom notice has been issued during the ongoing SIR, for being unmapped and for logical discrepancies, BLOs (booth-level officers) will visit the homes of such persons for collection of documents and thereafter upload them on the ECINet, for decision by the ERO.”
“Such persons need not be called for hearing to ERO/AERO office. Only in exceptional circumstances, as decided by the ERO, the hearing will be held preferably online. Any adult member of the family can be authorised by the elector to attend the hearing on their behalf, if required. Facilities for the online hearing are to be strengthened.”
As regards new voter registration, the EC maintained that the declaration form attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Supreme Court, but for non-SIR period, the forms appFmahalicable as per rules (the Registration of Electors Rules 1960) will be used for new voter inclusion.
Also read | Declaration part of Form 6 changed since SIR in Bihar
The other issue that had attracted the ire of the two Election Commissioners was the supposed centralisation of management of voter rolls through the ECINet portal, with field officers unable to access it in many cases.
The statement said that “A Committee headed by Sr. Deputy Election Commissioner (DEC) and including an independent expert from IIT/IIIT will review the ECINET to double-check that it complies with the provisions of the Acts and Rules and submit report to the Commission”. It added that henceforth, all the new initiatives about IT modules and portals will be discussed in the Committee of Officers (COO) before approval by the commission.
“Field officers have role-based access to the ECINET system as per their statutory powers. In case, any further flexibility is required by the field officers, that will be made operational,” it added.
The commission also extended the period for filing claims and objections for Delhi till October 30 and for Maharashtra till October 12.
Many other administrative measures were also announced. These include circulation of an advanced agenda and issuance of minutes for all of Commission’s meetings, completion of annual performance appraisal reports of all the officers within the stipulated time frame, approval of the commission for foreign trips of officers and compliance with all directions issued by the Commissioners to the officers of the Commission.
The Opposition, which has been seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, remained unimpressed with the statement. Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said: “The CEC thinks he can hide behind protocol. He stands exposed and is now petrified as an entire country seeks to hold him accountable.”
“The ongoing SIR which has turned to be method of massive disenfranchisement of several crores of India must be suspended immediately without delay. In the meantime, nothing short of the CEC’s resignation or prosecution will suffice”.

articles.title_orig: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.title_zh: Hurricane Nolo expected to bring heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii’s Big Island
articles.content_orig:
NAALEHU, Hawaii — Hurricane Nolo is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane in the Pacific Ocean over the weekend and unleash intense rain, the possibility of life-threatening flash flooding and dangerous surf for Hawaii’s Big Island.
Nolo was a Category 5 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 160 mph early Saturday, the National Hurricane Center said, as its outer rainbands hit the Big Island. Hurricane conditions are possible on the island, especially in areas with steep terrain, the weather service warned.
The storm was moving north-northwest at 10 mph on Saturday morning, but was expected to turn northeast and head toward Baja California Sur on Monday.
This marks the third hurricane in less than two months to whip past Hawaii (following Lala and Lowell ). The active Pacific hurricane season is likely due to a record-setting El Niño — a natural climate pattern characterized by a rise in sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific, which can spawn more intense and frequent cyclones there.
Tess Kala, a South Point resident who grew up in the area, said the back-to-back storms are a shock to locals.
“Honestly, this is the first like, whoa, what happened? We had a lot of family and friends that have lived here all their lives through generations and never experienced this before,” she said.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said Friday that President Donald Trump approved the state’s request for an emergency declaration to provide federal assistance for emergency protective measures across the state.
Mark Peters, a resident of seven years of Naalehu, on the Big Island’s southern tip, said the damage from the recent hurricanes has not been forgotten.
“It hurts me when I see friends and neighbors and people of this community that I know, and I just see it in their eyes, I hear it in their voices. We’ve been through a lot down here, and we still got a lot to go,” Peters said.
“We’re just getting started with our recovery. But to have yet another big storm hit us, and potentially even bigger than the last one, it’s difficult,” he said.
While he praised his community for its resilience, he said the people are still in need of basics like food and water, and many are in the process of reconstruction.
“We’re talking years. This is going to be a long recovery,” Peters said Friday.
He recalled driving through Waiohinu in the aftermath of Hurricane Lala and his “eyes getting wide open with all the damage, and the cars and houses moved and not where they’re supposed to be, and Waiohinu Park having buildings in the baseball field.”
Kala, the South Point resident, is preparing for Nolo by “moving everything away from the houses, tying things down, making sure that everything is hosed up and taped up as best as we possibly can.”
Nolo will bring periods of heavy rain that will continue across the Big Island and Maui over the weekend, and could trigger life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep terrain across eastern and southern portions of both the Big Island and Maui, the hurricane center said.
Nolo is forecast to dump 8 to 12 inches of rain on the eastern and southern parts of the Big Island, with maximum amounts up to 16 inches. Western portions of the Big Island could see 1 to 3 inches of rain, with maximum amounts of 6 inches. Meanwhile, Maui could see 4 to 6 inches, with maximum amounts of 8 inches, the National Hurricane Center said.
The rest of Hawaii will experience smaller rainfall totals, but isolated flooding is possible.
Nolo could also bring large and damaging waves along portions of the Big Island’s coastline into the weekend.
A hurricane watch and tropical storm warning are in effect for Hawaii County, and a tropical storm watch is in effect for Maui County. A hurricane watch means that hurricane conditions are possible within 24-36 hours. A wind advisory has been issued for the rest of the state.
Tropical storm-force winds will reach the Big Island on Friday afternoon, with hurricane-force winds possible by late evening.
A high surf advisory is in effect for the south- and east-facing shores of the Big Island and the east-facing shores of Maui and Molokai. A high-surf advisory was also issued for the east-facing shores of Niihau, Kauai and Oahu beginning Friday evening.
Nolo could also spawn tornadoes and large waterspouts over and near the Big Island and to the right of the track of the tropical cyclone.
Marlene Lenthang reported from Los Angeles, and Ryan Chandler and Shanshan Dong reported from Naalehu, Hawaii.

articles.title_orig: Nor’easter to bring rain, winds and flooding to the East Coast through the weekend
articles.title_zh: Nor’easter to bring rain, winds and flooding to the East Coast through the weekend
articles.content_orig:
New York’s governor declared a state of emergency and major concerts and events were canceled in the Northeast on Friday as a rare fall nor’easter began lashing the Atlantic coast.
Waves were crashing over seawalls in coastal New Jersey Friday afternoon, where the National Weather Service said winds were forecast to gust up to 60 mph and large breaking waves were expected to reach up to 9 feet.
More than 31 million people were under coastal flooding warnings or advisories. The strongest winds were expected through Saturday night on Long Island in New York and in New England.
In North Wildwood, New Jersey, tourists were recording video of the sea Friday as the storm approached. Some locals said they were worried about power outages in the coastal community.
“The weather is going to be crazy. It always is for a nor’easter,” said Chris Jenkins, who lives four blocks from the ocean.
Asked if she expected power outages, Jenkins had a simple answer: “Always.”
Her backup power sources were charged, and they have a fireplace in the home with logs in case the heat goes out.
In New York City, Global Citizen canceled its yearly festival in Central Park, and All Things Go, a music festival in Queens, did the same.
The AC/DC concert at MetLife Stadium, normally home to the New York Giants and Jets, was pushed to Oct. 2, and Ed Sheeran canceled his shows scheduled for Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts.
The New York Yankees squeezed in a doubleheader with the Orioles by moving Saturday’s game to Friday, and Saturday’s Boston Red Sox game was moved to Florida and will take place Sunday instead.
A travel advisory is in effect for New York City through Sunday, and people were advised to stay home and avoid unnecessary travel. It also urged residents to make sure catch basins were clear.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the coastal flooding was expected to be at its worst Saturday morning, especially around the Rockaways, the coast of Staten Island, and Jamaica Bay.
“If you live in a basement, know your exits and be ready to move if water approaches,” he said in a video Friday.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency, which helps in issuing aid, covering the New York City area and Long Island. Coastal flooding is the main concern, she said.
“Take this storm seriously,” she said in a statement .
Heavy rain bands — up to 4 to 6 inches — will hit the area Saturday and into Sunday, and winds will push water onto shore, with 1 to 4 feet of inundation expected.
Widespread 1 to 3 inches of rain is possible from the Interstate 95 corridor to the coast. The Jersey Shore, Long Island and coastal New England are likely to see the highest rain totals.
Waves of 10 to 18 feet are expected, with coastal flooding forecasts of 1 to 4 feet depending on the area.
By Saturday, rain will begin from the Jersey Shore to eastern Massachusetts and is expected to last all day.
Saturday will also feature the highest wind potential, with wind gusts that could reach 60 mph in coastal locations.
Rain will continue for the Northeast and New England on Sunday, as beaches continue to take a beating from the strong onshore winds.
The storm will still be spinning just off the coast Monday. While winds will be weaker, rain and beach erosion will continue.
Winds are expected to lead to travel delays and power outages into Monday.
Southeast New England faces the highest risk of power outages because of the strongest wind potential and top-heavy trees with leaves still on them.
Areas of New Jersey were already lashed by rough surf Friday morning, with videos showing waves crashing along the shore.
“The waves, the wave actions, the way it comes in, it just takes everything in its path,” said Mike Jones, the emergency management director for Upper Township, New Jersey. “And there’s really no way to stop Mother Nature.”
A full moon Saturday night is also expected to lift tides up to 5 to 6 inches.
One New Jersey resident said she closed up her whole house to prepare.
Outside Washington, abnormally high tides were seen along the Potomac River, inundating roads with floodwaters. Oceans Calling, a popular three-day music festival in Ocean City, Maryland, over three days, was canceled.
In North Carolina, winds greater than 50 mph have been recorded. A video showed a car in the state nearly swept into the ocean before a tow truck saved it.
Nor’easters are so called because the wind hitting the U.S. East Coast comes from the northeast. Cold air comes south from Canada and creates a storm when it meets warmer ocean water in the Atlantic, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says.
They are most common and most violent between September and April, and they “nearly always bring precipitation in the form of heavy rain or snow,” it says.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Nolo is churning toward Hawaii with 160 mph mph winds. It was a Category 5 hurricane early Saturday and was moving northwest at 10 mph. At some point over the weekend, it is expected to become a major hurricane, upgraded to a Category 3 or 4.
The storm will remain south of Hawaii, according to forecasters, but it will still affect the Big Island and Maui.
Outer rainbands were affecting the Big Island at around 5 p.m. local time (11 p.m. ET), and the island could get up to 16 inches of rain, the National Hurricane Center warned . People in Hawaii are preparing for the worst, expecting catastrophic flooding.
“Nolo is forecast to strengthen into a major hurricane this weekend, and could further intensify early next week,” the NHC said in a bulletin.
Just last month, Hurricane Lala brought destruction to Hawaii’s Big Island, damaging more than 100 homes and stranding people without water and power.
In addition to dangerous surf and damaging winds, mudslides are a major concern in the state.
As of Thursday night, stores were sold out of generators and gas cans. Shops were boarded up and blocked with sandbags. Schools were let out Thursday to give residents more time to prepare.

articles.title_orig: Huge crowds greet Pope in Paris for open-air Mass
articles.title_zh: Huge crowds greet Pope in Paris for open-air Mass
articles.content_orig:
Crowds line Place de la Concorde on second day of pontiff’s first official papal visit to France in 18 years
Hundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in ⁠Paris on Saturday to attend an open-air mass with Pope Leo, on the second day of his visit to France .
The Vatican estimated 700,000 people turned out for the outdoor mass with the 71-year-old American pope – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend.
It took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic.
The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life.
But cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked ‌God in his homily for the chance to ‌visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promote Catholicism and its teachings.
It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.
Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.”
He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness.
“Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said.
The security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.
Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances.
He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.
About 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops.
Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.”
Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”

George Russell held off Max Verstappen for his first win in three months to cut into Kimi Antonelli’s standings lead at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
Russell started on pole and built a big lead before having to defend on two safety car restarts, before holding off Verstappen, who charged through the field from eighth to second and nearly chased down the Briton on the final lap.
Verstappen remains winless this year for the first time since his rookie season in 2016. Verstappen’s Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar was third on his return from injury.
Antonelli started 16th after a crash in qualifying but ended up fifth as he limited the damage to his title lead, swerving to avoid a three-car crash ahead of him and later overtaking Lewis Hamilton.

“Win every race. My team-mate has had an incredible season, he’s been pretty flawless and now we’re getting to crunch time. I am going to focus on myself. It’s been a real tough period for me and I feel like I have come through the other side.”

articles.content_orig:
The Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend went the way many believed the 2026 season would play out. Russell strolled to victory from pole, though with a little late jeopardy, whilst Kimi Antonelli’s crash in qualifying meant he had to fight his way through the field to finish fifth. That, after all, was the order of things last season.
Yet the past few days in Baku are an inversion of the season’s storyline. It is Antonelli who has been the faster driver, heading for a maiden world title at the second time of asking. Russell has been the troubled one. This was only the Briton’s third victory of the season and his first since Austria in late June. Antonelli has racked up eight wins and, before this weekend in Baku, a well-deserved 81-point lead over Russell.
Russell’s dominant and impressive run from pole to the chequered flag on Saturday is both a reminder of what he is capable of and also what might have been, had he been able to find this type of form earlier and more often. The reality, though, is that he needs to replicate this for the rest of the season to even be in with a sniff, barring a catastrophic meltdown from Antonelli. Still, Russell looked elated to have ended his barren run.
The finish was a little more tense than Russell deserved, having established a healthy lead in the first half of the race. Two late safety cars eradicated his advantage and helped put Max Verstappen’s Red Bull on his gearbox. In the end, he triumphed by just under 0.2sec and, as Antonelli finished fifth – with some help from two safety-car inducing crashes – he made up 15 points on his Mercedes team-mate. Isack Hadjar completed the podium for Red Bull after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.
A drag race to the finish line! 🍿 #F1 #AzerbaijanGP pic.twitter.com/Nb6xfkkpIb
Whether or not this performance is too little from Russell, it is almost certainly too late. The margin to the championship leader is now down to 66 points with a probable seven rounds – including one sprint race – remaining. It improves Russell’s chances of a championship from “unthinkable” to “remote”.
Russell has already written off his own hopes of beating Antonelli to the championship. He did not seem to have changed his mind or his approach after stepping out of his car victoriously.
“Win every race. That’s the game plan,” Russell said. “My team-mate’s had an incredible season, he’s been pretty flawless throughout, but now we’re getting to crunch time.
“I’m just going to focus on myself. If I continue giving performances like I did this weekend, at the end of the season I’ll be happy because it’s been a tough period for me and I’ll feel like I’ve come through the other side.”
In fairness to Russell, his eighth grand prix victory did not come entirely out of nowhere as he has been much closer to Antonelli since the summer break. With a bit more luck in Zandvoort and Monza, he may have been closer still.
“I think it’s just having more experience with this new driving style I’ve adopted and every race since the break I feel like I’ve gone from strength to strength. I feel more like myself again,” he added.
Russell would have had an easier route to victory were it not for the two safety car periods in the second half of the race. The first came out after Alexander Albon slammed his Williams into the barriers at turn five on lap 31 of 51. That bunched the pack up and wiped out the 10-second lead that Russell had built up over Oscar Piastri’s McLaren.
As is so often the case in F1, and especially on street circuits, one safety car often brings about another. And so it was as Franco Colapinto’s enormously optimistic divebomb up the inside of turn one on the lap-36 restart took out not only his team-mate Pierre Gasly, but also Lando Norris.
Absolute chaos at the restart 😵 #F1 #AzerbaijanGP pic.twitter.com/o4Q5MdHLnc
Norris had stern words for Colapinto, who has been handed a five-place grid drop for the next race in Malaysia, after his elimination. “There’s just some drivers that shouldn’t be in Formula One, to be honest,” the reigning world champion said.
“I think the FIA should start handing out bans for this kind of stuff. It’s careless, it costs a lot of money. All my parts are in the bin,” he added.
The greatest pressure Russell faced came after the second restart, after Verstappen moved swiftly into second. The Dutchman, who has yet to win in 2026, is not a driver anybody wants to see fill their mirrors at the best of times, let alone when trying to end a 12-week, six-race win drought.
Yet Verstappen could not find a way past. The most threatening moment of the final 12 laps was on the final push to the chequered flag. Valtteri Bottas put his Cadillac in the wall, bringing out double-waved yellow flags at turn 15. Russell lost his electrical boost on the run to the line but managed to hold off Verstappen by just 0.196sec, the closest winning margin for more than two decades.
As for Antonelli? He surely just needs to keep his car out of the wall, whatever Russell does.

Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.
Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building.
Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.
All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, news agency Reuters reported citing local police.
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.

articles.title_orig: Chris Hansen Reacts To Seeing Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’
articles.title_zh: Chris Hansen Reacts To Seeing Robert Pattinson’s ‘Primetime’
articles.content_orig:
Chris Hansen found some fellow Primetime haters to share his displeasure with after he sat through the film, in which Robert Pattinson plays Hansen hosting To Catch a Predator .
Hansen caught Primetime on opening night after expressing his displeasure with the film and filmmakers in the weeks leading up to the release. Hansen objected to producers not reaching out to him and claimed he was asked to sign an unusual NDA before he could attend a screening.
Hansen did not sign that NDA and caught the A24 film with a regular New York crowd. The longtime reporter said no one recognized him before the film.
"It was so bizarre and so in and out of reality," Hansen said in a first reaction outside the theater.
"It's hard for me to — you know, obviously I'm not objective because the character is me, but it was so detached from reality or anything I've ever experienced, then or now, doing the investigations. I just think it's — I'm not sure what the point of it was."
Hansen released his fuller thoughts and his conversation with other moviegoers on the latest episode of his Have a Seat podcast, where he invited Fox News' Jesse Watters to temporarily take over hosting duties.
Some who talked to Hansen praised the intensity of the movie, but many also just echoed Hansen's complaints about it not being realistic.
"It's very intense, very kind of gut-wrenching dramatic," one moviegoer said, though he later said it was "absurd" that the movie tried to portray Hansen as worse than some of the predators he caught in his investigations.
"Well, I watch a lot of your stuff on YouTube. I felt like it was very over dramatized," another viewer said.
"I happen to agree with you," Hansen said.
"The morals of it were stripped away from it," one woman said, later adding, "I don't think it's doing anyone a favor by demonizing taking down predators."
Another told Hansen, "I don't like the depiction of how it showed you."
A couple more viewers said they didn't feel it demonized Hansen in the way they thought it would.
Expanding his thoughts on the movie with Watters, Hansen called it "pure fiction," saying the timeline of the show's run is not how it happened, and he objected to specific exchanges between the fictional Hansen and one of his decoy actors.
He was also critical of Pattinson's performance of him, saying he was portraying a detached man having a mental breakdown of sorts.
"In a way, it's a hit piece on me and the series, which is weird because all we do is expose bad human beings who try to hurt children. So in that respect, it's sort of an insult to the thousands of men and women who walk every day to do the same things that I try to do and take down and get in to catch a predator. But I think it's so far over the top," Hansen said.
On Pattinson, Hansen added about his performance, "I think it's overly dramatic, drawn out. They make him look like a character in a horror film. There's all kinds of green hue on his face. He's obviously having a mental breakdown. "

articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has rejected Iran's conditional proposal for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, telling aides he expects to resume bombing the country after November's midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported Saturday, quoting unnamed U.S. officials.
In a gaggle with reporters later on Saturday, Trump confirmed he had rejected Iran's latest offer: "They made a proposal but I rejected it."
Meanwhile, Yemen's Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted projectiles fired by Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Friday proposed reopening the strategically vital strait and resuming nuclear talks with the U.S. within seven days if the Trump administration accepts its conditions.
"If certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz will be open at the end of seven days, and talks will be restarted," Araghchi told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
Tehran's conditions include a halt to what it calls U.S. "acts of aggression," an end to the naval blockade and economic warfare, and the release of Iranian assets, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said this week.
Trump said earlier this month that he expects the war, which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iran, to end shortly after the midterms and for oil prices to fall afterward.
But privately, Trump is skeptical Iran would meet his demands and has told his staff that he sees a renewed bombing campaign as likely, the WSJ quoted officials as saying.
CNBC could not immediately confirm the report.
The Journal quoted a U.S. official as saying Washington and Tehran were still negotiating through mediators, including over U.S. demands intended to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon.
Though direct fighting between U.S. and Iranian forces has been greatly reduced in recent weeks, Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have stepped up their attacks on their neighbor and U.S. ally Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi-backed Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen "intercepted and destroyed" two drones launched by Houthi militia towards the Saudi capital Riyadh, and two ballistic missiles aimed at the Khamis Mushait region near the city of Abha in the country's southwest, Colonel Turki Al-Maliki, the coalition's official spokesman, said in a series of posts on X.
The Houthis said last Saturday that they had attacked "sensitive" sites in Riyadh shortly after flames and smoke were seen near the city's main airport. Saudi Arabia said earlier this month that its air defenses destroyed a Houthi drone headed for the holy city of Mecca, a claim the group denied.
The war has severely restricted energy shipments out of the Middle East, sending oil prices soaring and raising concerns about accelerating inflation globally.
But crude prices posted a sharp drop for the week as Tehran and Washington held discussions on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.
West Texas Intermediate dropped 2.3% to close at $92.41 per barrel. Brent , the international benchmark, declined 2.1% to settle at $104.32. U.S. crude finished the week 7.9% lower while Brent was flat.
WTI is up nearly 61% year to date, while Brent crude is more than 71% higher over the same period.

articles.title_orig: Outrage as East German town bans Holocaust ‘stumbling blocks’
articles.title_zh: Outrage as East German town bans Holocaust ‘stumbling blocks’
articles.content_orig:
There has been outrage after a small town in eastern Germany banned the installation of new Holocaust memorial plaques that mark the last known residence or workplace of Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution.
‘Stolpersteine,’ meaning ‘stumbling blocks’, are found across Germany, as well as in other European countries, and are intended as a daily reminder of Nazi atrocities.
The motion was proposed by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), who argued that passersby are “walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims.” On Thursday, the city council of Heidenau, a town near Dresden in Saxony, backed the motion.
The parties’ local branches instead proposed that future Holocaust commemorations should be kept at the town’s memorial site at its northern cemetery, German media report. CNN has approached both parties for comment.
The move has sparked backlash, with opponents arguing that part of the purpose of the memorials is their subtle intrusion into everyday life.
The small 10cm brass cubes, often installed in sidewalks outside residential homes, are the work of German artist Gunter Demnig who initiated the project in the 1990s.
They all carry similar information, such as the individual’s name, date of deportation, and place of death. To date 116,000 plaques have been installed across 31 countries, the vast majority are in Germany.
Demnig himself has rejected the recent motion in Heidenau. Speaking to German media, he said that the blocks must be visible in the specific locations where people used to live or work, and that they help bring history to life for young people.
He said he was not surprised by the ban, given the AfD’s recent electoral successes, and said of the CDU that the party “should perhaps drop its ‘C’. Because they’ve clearly left Christianity behind.”
Felix Banaszak, co-leader of Germany’s Green Party, described it as a scandal and said that the reasoning that people were stepping on the blocks was “absurd.”
“They bring the names and fates of the victims into our everyday lives and prompt us to pause for a moment,” he told German media.
Charlotte Knobloch, the president of a Jewish association in Bavaria and a Holocaust survivor herself, described the town council’s decision as the “completely wrong path.”
Speaking to Germany’s Funke Media Group, she said that while she herself was not a friend of the ‘Stolpersteine’ concept, “decentralized commemoration that is not banished from public spaces” is key for the country’s culture of remembrance.
The AfD has long challenged Germany’s forms of commemoration of the atrocities committed under Adolf Hitler.
In Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD recently sealed it best-ever win in state elections, a prominent AfD official described their vision to overhaul the state’s school history lessons as “more Bismark – less Hitler.”
On a federal level, the party was designated as a far-right extremist organization by German domestic intelligence, although that designation is currently under review. Individuals within the party have also been accused of being extremists.
Aside from the fact that a far-right policy has been approved at the local level in Germany, the move lays bare a growing issue in German politics; adherence to the ‘Brandmauer,’ or firewall, an informal position for mainstream parties that sees them rule out cooperation with the AfD.
This firewall, which is designed to keep the far right out of political decision making and stifle their growth, is under serious pressure. The CDU’s willingness to work together with the AfD to pass this motion has sparked criticism of the CDU leadership and comes at a time when the Chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz is already facing a crisis over poor performances in recent regional elections.
The International Auschwitz Committee slammed the CDU’s support of the motion as scandalous, according to Deutsche Welle.
“This is a transparent and despicable attempt to drive Nazi victims in Heidenau out of the city once again and dispose of them where, according to the AfD, their memory has belonged a long time ago — at the cemetery,” the committee’s executive vice president said.

articles.title_orig: Six Dead After Explosion in Athens Tourist District
articles.title_zh: Six Dead After Explosion in Athens Tourist District
articles.content_orig:
The building in the Plaka district was reduced to rubble strewn with household items
Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.
The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.
Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building.
Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.
All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."
The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.
The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.
Investigators at the scene believe the blast was caused by a gas leak
Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.
Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.
The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.
A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are aware of a suspected explosion in Athens and are in touch with the local authorities."

articles.title_orig: Week in Politics: Trump faces Republican defections; U.S.-China summit; press feud
articles.title_zh: Week in Politics: Trump faces Republican defections; U.S.-China summit; press feud
articles.content_orig:
Some GOP candidates are stepping back from unpopular Trump administration policies. Meanwhile, a U.S.-China summit at the White House and tensions with the press corps.
At the Republican National Convention in Dallas last month, ahead of the midterms, President Trump asked his supporters...
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: To pretend that I'm on the ballot. I'm on the ballot. I'm on it.
SIMON: Some Republican candidates, especially in competitive races, don't have to pretend and are trying to step away from some of President Trump's most unpopular policies.
(SOUNDBITE OF PRESS CONFERENCE)
ASHLEY HINSON: I've called for an immediate and successful end to the war in Iran so that families can see some relief at the pump and at the checkout line.
SIMON: That's Ashley Hinson, the Iowa Republican running for the Senate, speaking at a press conference yesterday. NPR political reporter Elena Moore joins us. Elena, thanks so much for being with us.
ELENA MOORE, BYLINE: Good morning, Scott.
SIMON: Thirty-eight days until Election Day. What is increasing Republicans' worry over being associated with President Trump?
MOORE: Well, you know, Democrats have been campaigning on the need to address rising costs throughout the midterm cycle, but I think that message only got louder once the war in Iran began. And Trump's defended his decision to go to war, but it's tricky for Republicans on the ballot this far - this fall - because the war is unpopular. You know, voters are worried about how the conflict is affecting the cost of gas and groceries.
But this week, we did - as you said, we saw several GOP candidates who are running in these tight, competitive races directly make that connection, like Ashley Hinson in Iowa. This message shift makes sense if you look at the polls, which show Republicans trailing Democrats on the generic ballot. And, you know, the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll has Democrats up by 12 points over Republicans.
SIMON: And the shift in messaging is interesting, given the premium that President Trump puts on loyalty.
MOORE: Oh, yeah. I mean, he's always put this emphasis on party loyalty. But, you know, he's kind of in a different era of his political career right now, you can argue. Trump is a lame duck, and he's also facing, like, you know, historically low popularity among voters. Which is important to note because Trump has repeatedly, like you said, told voters to act like he's on the ballot this fall. And, you know, that's something that, once again, could put GOP candidates trying to appeal to moderates and independents in a tough situation.
SIMON: The President hosted a three-day summit in Washington, D.C., with China's President Xi Jinping this week. What do you note about the visit?
MOORE: Well, yeah. I mean, there was a lot of pageantry. You know, there was a big state dinner. Trump gave Xi a private tour of the South Lawn, and they literally rolled out the red carpet for his arrival. As for what came out of the meetings between China and the U.S., it doesn't appear to be much. The U.S. has said it's extending a trade truce with China for two months. But, Scott, there's still a lot of unanswered questions about what this relationship between these two countries looks like moving forward.
For one, the summit comes amid rising concerns about what the U.S. and global leaders should do when it comes to regulating AI. But Trump has repeatedly pushed back on that, saying the U.S. needs to stay in competition with China. So, you know, likely more to come there. And we should also say Xi and Trump are expected to see each other two more times before the end of the year at different geopolitical events.
SIMON: And a big story playing out in court this week after the president banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. Where do things stand right now?
MOORE: I mean, there was a lot of back and forth on this story throughout the week. A few days ago, a federal judge ruled that the White House had to give access back, at least temporarily. But the fight continues. As of last night - Friday night - the White House barred CNN from traveling aboard Air Force One today as the president goes to Tennessee for a college football game. And, Scott, what makes this extra complicated is CNN was supposed to be the TV press pooler today. And that can really matter.
You know, Trump has always had this love-hate relationship with the legacy news media. He rags on them. He says, fake news. But every day, the White House press pool plays a pretty big role in disseminating information about the president. They travel with him. They cover his events, and they quickly share video and audio that often ends up on national broadcasts. And at points this week, as several major news outlets boycotted doing pool duties or broadcasting that footage, it meant Trump, who is and has always been a showman, got less airtime.
SIMON: NPR's political reporter Elena Moore. Thanks so much for coming in to see us today.
